path.title: Data Science and Analysis
path.subtitle: From spreadsheet to signal — without the PhD
path.summary: Most analysts spend half their day cleaning data and the other half pretending they did not. This path teaches the actual job: forming a question, surviving the cleaning, doing the right test on a sample of 47 not 4700, and writing a memo your CFO will read in 90 seconds. By the end you can take a vague "figure out why" prompt and ship a defensible answer.

The trap: p-hacking and confirmation bias

blocks.md:
Most analyst careers begin the same way: a manager forwards an Excel file with the subject line *"can you take a quick look at this?"* and three minutes of context. You open the file, scroll, sigh, and start a pivot table. By Wednesday you have produced 11 charts and answered no question.

The job you think you have is *finding insights in data*. The job you actually have is *converting a vague human question into a testable one, and then producing the smallest useful piece of evidence*. The data is the easy part. The translation is the hard part. Everything in this course follows from getting that order right.

blocks.title: Mental model: question becomes hypothesis becomes test
blocks.md:
Hold this picture. Every piece of analysis is a chain of three things in this order: a vague human **question**, a testable **hypothesis** that converts the question into something the data can answer, and a **test** that produces yes / no / cannot tell. The chain only runs forwards.

If you start with the data, you skip steps 1 and 2 and produce charts that decorate a question nobody asked. If you start with a hypothesis but no question, you answer the wrong thing precisely. The discipline is: never touch the file until you can write the question on a sticky note.

blocks.caption: The translation moment in motion. Watch a one-line stakeholder ask convert into three candidate hypotheses, and only one survives the data check.

hi-IN.title: Manager-meeting wala scene
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, scene yeh hai. Manager ne aake pucha *"is this significant?"*. Tu ne dashboard kholke bola *"p = 0.04 hai sir"*. Manager ne head hilaaya, *"good, ship it"* bolke nikal gaya. 

Dono mein se kisi ko nahi pata kya ship hua. Tu ne effect size nahi bataya. Usne business threshold nahi pucha. Lekin meeting khatam, dashboard banane wala bhi happy, decision lene wala bhi happy. **Yeh data science nahi hai. Yeh data theatre hai.**

en.title: The standup that decides nothing
en.md: Manager asks 'is this significant?'. You say 'p = 0.04'. Manager says 'good, ship it'. Neither of you knows what was just shipped, what effect size matters, or whether the change is worth the engineering cost. The meeting felt productive; nothing was actually decided. This pattern repeats four times a week in most analytics teams.

blocks.caption: Watch (~30s) · The two questions data answers (only) — descriptive vs predictive split.

blocks.md:
Every dataset is a stack of two things mashed together: **signal** (the underlying truth) and **noise** (random variation, measurement error, edge cases, holiday weeks, that one bug in event tracking last Tuesday). Your job is to separate them. Most analysts skip this step and report the noise as if it were the signal.

A Mumbai fintech I work with had a 14% week-over-week revenue jump in March. Champagne emoji in Slack. Turned out the previous week had a feature flag bug that nulled out 30% of the events. The signal was *flat revenue*; the 14% was *measurement noise from a previously corrupt week*. They almost wrote a board update on it. The noise-vs-signal lens is asking, before any other question, *what could make this number look the way it does that has nothing to do with what I think it means?*

blocks.title: The translation: 'why is churn up?' becomes a test in 6 steps

steps.label: Step 1 — Hear the question
steps.body: CMO says 'why is churn up'. Resist the urge to open the dashboard. The question, as stated, has at least three definitions of 'churn' and no time window.

steps.label: Step 2 — Restate it
steps.body: Write it down: 'Did the monthly churn rate (paid_users that did not renew within 30 days of contract end) increase from Q2 to Q3 by more than 1 percentage point?'

steps.label: Step 3 — Confirm with the asker
steps.body: Send it to the CMO. Get her to say yes or correct the definition. This is the part most analysts skip and most analysts regret.

steps.label: Step 4 — Form a hypothesis
steps.body: From the question, generate 2-3 testable hypotheses. e.g. 'Tier B users churned more in Q3 than Q2'. Each one is a comparison the data can run.

steps.label: Step 5 — Pick the test
steps.body: For a comparison of two cohorts on a binary outcome, a chi-square or two-proportion z-test, with sample size and CI reported. Not a vibes-based eyeball.

steps.label: Step 6 — Run it, with the noise check first
steps.body: Before reporting, ask: 'what could make this number look this way and not be churn?' Holiday week, data outage, definition change, billing migration. If any of those, the answer is 'data quality first, churn second'.

blocks.prompt: Your dashboard shows weekly active users dropped 12% last week. What is the most disciplined first move?

choices.label: Ask 'what could make this number look this way that has nothing to do with usage?' — check for tracking outages, definition changes, holiday weeks, deploys
choices.explain: Correct. The noise-vs-signal lens. Big jumps are often artifacts; you investigate the artifact first or you ship a wrong story.

choices.label: Email the CEO that engagement is dropping
choices.explain: Premature alarm. You do not yet know if the number reflects user behaviour or a data bug. The escalation costs more than the 30 minutes of investigation.

choices.label: Build a churn model
choices.explain: Modeling on possibly-corrupt data. You will fit a model to a tracking outage and explain it confidently.

choices.label: Add more metrics to the dashboard
choices.explain: Same dirty source, more charts. Does not address the question.

hi-IN.title: Confirmation bias ka EMI
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, ek baar tujhe lagta hai *"Tier B users zyaada churn karte hain"*, tu data mein utar jaata hai aur surprise — Tier B users zyaada churn karte dikhte hain. Tu 200 hypotheses mein se sirf woh dekhta hai jo confirm karte hain. Yeh **confirmation bias** ka EMI hai: har month dimaag ko thoda aur convince karta hai, aur kabhi pre-pay nahi karna padta.

Bachne ka tarika: hypothesis pehle likh, data baad mein khol. Sticky note pe, ya Slack DM mein khud ko, kuch bhi. Likha hua hypothesis revise karna padta hai. Soche hue hypothesis aaram se shift ho jaate hain.

en.title: Confirmation bias on monthly EMI
en.md: Once you suspect 'Tier B users churn more', you will see exactly that pattern in the data. Confirmation bias is on a monthly EMI plan: every analysis pays a small instalment, and you never have to face the principal. The fix is to write the hypothesis down before opening the data. Written hypotheses get revised; remembered ones quietly drift to fit the chart.

blocks.caption: Watch (~30s) · Where the day actually goes — the time-spent stack.

blocks.md:
If you cannot write the question on one line, you cannot answer it. The rule is brutal and non-negotiable: before you open the file, write the question down. Numerically. With the time window. With the metric definition. With the comparison.

*"How is the product doing?"* is not a question. *"Did 30-day retention for paid users on the Pro plan in Q3 2026 increase or decrease relative to Q2 2026, by more than 1pp?"* is a question. The first one will absorb 4 hours of work and produce nothing useful. The second one is answerable by Tuesday lunch. They sound similar; they are not.

coach.name: Senior-DS Saanya
coach.role: Tech lead at a Bengaluru SaaS, 9 years of cleaning other people's data

intro: Hey. I'm Saanya. I run the data team at a B2B SaaS, and I have spent more time decoding stakeholder questions than running models. 👋
I'm going to throw five real-shaped stakeholder questions at you. Tell me which bucket each one belongs in.
**Stated** = ready to answer. **Needs translation** = restate before touching data. **Push back** = the question is malformed; do not answer until it changes.

scenarios.situation: CMO Slack: 'churn went up — figure out why by Thursday'
scenarios.explain: Vague but answerable. Translate first: which churn definition, which cohort, which time window, what's the threshold for 'went up'. Confirm with the CMO before opening the file.

scenarios.situation: PM ticket: 'Did the new pricing tier (Pro+) retain at the same 30-day rate as Pro in the first 6 weeks after launch (Sep 1 – Oct 13, 2026)? Threshold: ≥ -2pp.'
scenarios.explain: Numeric, time-windowed, threshold stated, cohorts defined. This is what a stated question looks like. Skip translation, run the comparison.

scenarios.situation: CFO: 'Are we doing better than last year?'
scenarios.explain: Better at what? Revenue, retention, NPS, headcount efficiency? Translate before answering. Send 3 candidate definitions, ask which one she means.

scenarios.situation: VP Sales: 'Prove that our top-tier customers are also our happiest.'
scenarios.explain: 'Prove' is the giveaway. The question pre-supposes the answer and asks you to confirm it. That is a confirmation-bias trap masquerading as analysis. Push back: 'I can test whether tier and satisfaction are correlated; I cannot promise to prove a direction.'

scenarios.situation: Engineering manager: 'Is the new caching layer making the app feel faster?'
scenarios.explain: Translate to a measurable: median page-load latency, 95th percentile, time-to-interactive. Then a before/after comparison. 'Feel' is not measurable; latency is.

scenarios.situation: CEO: 'Tell me a story about the data.'
scenarios.explain: Not a question; an open-ended request that absorbs unbounded time. Push back: 'I can give you the top 3 movements this quarter with one chart each. Which framing fits — what's working, what's broken, or what's changing?'

blocks.title: The classic trap: p-hacking and confirmation bias
blocks.md:
The two most common ways an analysis lies to the analyst:

1. **p-hacking**: running enough tests until one of them reports p < 0.05, then writing up that one as 'the' result. Run 20 tests at α=0.05 and roughly one will look significant by chance. This is statistical fraud, even when accidental.
2. **Confirmation bias**: forming a belief, then noticing only the data that supports it. The fix is to write the hypothesis *before* you look, and be loud about which evidence would have changed your mind.

Both traps share the same root: you let the data search for the conclusion instead of the conclusion specifying the test. The discipline of writing the question down first is the cheapest defence against both.

blocks.prompt: Order the steps of a disciplined analysis loop, from first to last.

items.label: Restate as a numeric, testable hypothesis
Confirm with the asker before touching data
items.detail: Send the restatement; get a yes.

items.label: Apply the noise-vs-signal lens
items.detail: Ask: what could explain this number that is NOT what I think?

items.label: Run the test on a clean sample
items.detail: Pick the appropriate test; report effect size and CI, not just p.

items.label: Write the BLUF answer with assumption ledger

blocks.hint: Each step's output is the next step's input. The classic mistake is to skip 'confirm with the asker' and jump from 'restate' straight to 'run the test'.

blocks.instruction:
Take this real-shaped stakeholder ask and convert it into a stated question in the format `metric / cohort / window / threshold / comparator`.

*"Hey, I think our SMB customers in Hyderabad are using the product less than they used to. Can you check?"*
blocks.expected:
metric: weekly active sessions per account (or product-defined 'usage')
cohort: SMB-tier accounts based in Hyderabad (city = Hyderabad in account.city)
window: last 8 weeks vs the 8 weeks before that (or Q3 2026 vs Q2 2026)
threshold: ≥10% drop in median weekly active sessions per account to count as 'using less'
comparator: Wilcoxon signed-rank or two-sample t-test on per-account session counts, reported with 95% CI and effect size

blocks.prompt: A teammate runs 14 different segment tests, finds one with p = 0.03, and writes it up as the headline finding. Which problems are present?

choices.label: p-hacking — reporting only the significant test from a search of many
choices.explain: Correct. With 14 tests at α=0.05, you expect about one to look significant by chance even if no real effect exists. Reporting only that one without correction is the textbook trap.

choices.label: Confirmation bias — the search likely stopped at the first result that looked good
choices.explain: Correct. The search-and-stop pattern. The 14 tests are not equal; you stopped searching when you found what you wanted to find.

choices.label: Sample size too small
choices.explain: Maybe also a problem, but not the central issue here. The headline failure is the search pattern, not the n.

choices.label: Wrong choice of model
choices.explain: Not the issue — the problem is procedural, not modeling-class.

hi-IN.title: Mummy ka cross-examination
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, mummy se data science seekh. Tu boltaa hai *"market jaake aata hoon"*. Mummy: *"kis market? kab tak? kya laana hai? kitna budget? Sharma ji ke saath ya akele?"*

Voh tujhe stated question banane sikha rahi hai. Tu ne *vague mission* boli, mummy ne *metric, window, cohort, threshold, comparator* maanga. Stakeholder bhi yahi karna chahiye, lekin agar voh nahi karta, **tu kar.**

en.title: Your mother is the senior analyst
en.md: Tell your mother 'I'm going to the market'. She'll ask: which market, how long, what for, with what budget, alone or with someone. That is a stakeholder forcing you to convert a vague mission into a stated question. Stakeholders should do this; usually they don't. So you do.

blocks.title: Field Notes: 47 Tests, One Headline, Zero Replication
blocks.source: Anonymous senior analyst at Paisa Vault, a Pune-based consumer-fintech startup
blocks.story:
On March 11, 2025, the growth-analytics team at Paisa Vault published a celebrated internal note titled *"Why Tier-2 Cities Convert 1.8x Better Than Tier-1."* It went up on the company wiki, got pinned in #all-hands, and was quoted by the CEO in the next investor update. The methodology section, in tiny font on page 4, read: *"Logistic regression with city-tier as predictor; p = 0.043."*

What the note did not mention: the same analyst had run **47 hypothesis tests** that week against the same Q4 dataset. Tier, age bucket, gender, device type, referral source, time-of-day, day-of-week, NPS bucket, lifetime-value decile, and 38 others. **One** of them, by sheer luck of the multiple-comparisons fairy, came in at p < 0.05. That one became *"the finding."* The other 46 went into the recycle bin.

In April, the product team rolled out a Tier-2 acquisition push based on the note. Six weeks of paid marketing, ₹38 lakh of spend. **Conversion lift: -0.4 percent.** Replication on Q1 data: p = 0.71. The growth lead, in the post-mortem on May 2, said the line that everyone now quotes back: *"We didn't have a finding. We had a coincidence with a confidence interval."*

The analyst still works there. The note is still on the wiki, with a banner now: *"RETRACTED — see post-mortem."*
blocks.takeaway: If you torture a dataset long enough, it will confess to anything. State your hypothesis before you touch the data, or don't dignify what comes out as a finding.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: Is Churn Really Up?
blocks.setup:
It's **Day 4** of Aditi's first week at Vyapaar Money, a Mumbai consumer-credit fintech. She has a fresh laptop, a still-sticky onboarding mug, and Slack DM from her boss at 9:47am: *"Quick one. The leadership offsite is Friday. Is churn really up this quarter? Need a one-liner I can put on a slide. Thanks!"*

Aditi opens the data warehouse. She has access to 14 tables, three years of history, and exactly **48 hours**. She pings you, her unofficial mentor.

coach.name: Staff-DS Sandeep
coach.role: Staff data scientist, six startups in, allergic to dashboards without denominators

stages.prompt: Aditi types: *"I'll just pull churn rate by month for Q3 and Q2, eyeball it, send the number."* What do you tell her **first**?

options.label: "Sounds good, ship it. Sandeep is busy."
options.explain: Sandeep watches Aditi's slide land in Friday's deck with the words *churn is up 14 percent.* Three weeks later the cohort team finds it was a denominator change — the product redefined 'active user' in August. Aditi's slide is now in a board memo. Sandeep emails her, gently.

options.label: "Before you query: write down what 'churn is up' would actually have to look like in the data to be true. Then go look."
options.explain: **Yes.** Hypothesis first, data second. Aditi writes: *churn is up = the cohort-adjusted 90-day retention curve in Q3 sits below the same curve in Q2 by more than the noise of the last 6 quarters.* Now she knows what query to write and what answer would actually settle it.

options.label: "Run 20 cuts of the data — by city, age, plan, device — and find the most dramatic chart."
options.explain: This is the Paisa Vault playbook from the field notes. Run enough cuts and one will look dramatic by chance alone. Aditi will ship a coincidence and call it a finding. Hard pass.

options.label: "Just ask the boss what answer he wants and back into it."
options.explain: Sandeep would like a word. This is how analysts become rubber stamps and then get blamed in retros for findings that weren't theirs to begin with.

stages.prompt: Aditi writes the hypothesis. She pulls Q2 and Q3 churn. Q2: 4.1 percent. Q3: 4.6 percent. She's about to Slack: *"churn up 12 percent QoQ."* What do you say?

options.label: "Looks decisive. Send it."
options.explain: 12 percent relative jump on a base of 4 percent is well inside the noise band of a quarterly metric on a fintech with seasonality. She's about to call a wave a tide.

options.label: "What's the quarter-on-quarter noise floor for the last 8 quarters? If Q1 to Q2 also moved 12 percent in random directions, this isn't a signal."
options.explain: **Exactly.** Aditi pulls the historical series and finds Q-on-Q swings of -9, +14, -6, +11, -3, +8, -7 percent over the last two years. Q3's +12 is unremarkable. The 'finding' dissolves on contact with context.

options.label: "Run a t-test on daily churn rates across the two quarters, report the p-value."
options.explain: A t-test on daily churn rates with n in the thousands will return p < 0.001 on tiny effect sizes that don't matter. She'll get statistical significance and zero practical significance. Wrong tool for the question.

options.label: "Segment by acquisition cohort first — a mix shift in new users can fake a churn spike."
options.explain: **Smart.** If Vyapaar acquired a flood of low-quality referral users in late Q2, Q3 churn looks worse without the underlying retention curve changing at all. Cohort-adjust before you call it a trend.

stages.prompt: Aditi cohort-adjusts. The Q3 curve is 0.3 points below Q2 — well inside historical noise. Boss wants a one-liner. **What does she write?**

options.label: "Churn is up 12 percent QoQ." (one number, no caveats)
options.explain: Confidently wrong. The number is real but the framing is misleading. Cohort-adjusted, there's no signal. This sentence will outlive the truth in every deck for the next six quarters.

options.label: "Headline churn ticked up from 4.1 to 4.6 percent QoQ, but cohort-adjusted retention is flat — within historical noise. No real change yet."
options.explain: **Ship this.** Specific numbers, the apparent move, the corrected interpretation, and a calibrated conclusion. Boss can put this on a slide and defend it from any VP who pulls on the thread.

options.label: "Churn analysis is complicated. Need more time."
options.explain: The work is done. This is a confidence problem masquerading as a thoroughness problem. Boss reads this as 'Aditi can't summarize.'

options.label: "Cohort-adjusted retention is flat. The 12 percent headline move is a mix-shift artifact from the June referral campaign."
options.explain: **Even better — names the cause.** If Aditi can point to the mechanism (June referral cohort dragging down headline numbers without affecting underlying retention), the boss now has a *story*, not just a number. That's a senior-analyst move.

outcomes.perfect: You walked Aditi from 'pull a number' to 'state a hypothesis, check the noise floor, cohort-adjust, write a defensible one-liner' in under two days. Sandeep buys you a vada pav. This is what a data mental model looks like in practice.
outcomes.good: Decent instincts on most of it. The hypothesis-first reflex is the muscle worth building — re-read the lesson on framing before the next ad-hoc request, because the next one is already in your DMs.
outcomes.learn: Aditi shipped a slide that didn't survive contact with a curious VP. Re-read the lesson — especially the section on **stating the hypothesis before querying** and **noise floors before headlines**. The Paisa Vault retraction is a preview, not a punchline.

points: Data science is the discipline of converting a vague human question into a testable one, not the discipline of running tests on data you happen to have.
If you cannot write the question on one line — metric, cohort, window, threshold, comparator — you cannot answer it.
Every dataset is signal plus noise; before you report a number, ask what could make it look this way that has nothing to do with what you think it means.
Write the hypothesis down before you open the data; spoken hypotheses drift to fit the chart, written ones get revised honestly.
p-hacking and confirmation bias share one root — letting data search for the conclusion — and one cheap fix: pre-register the test and report what would change your mind.

audioChapters.label: The trap: skip EDA, jump to modeling

blocks.md:
There is a famous statistic that 80% of a data scientist's time is spent on cleaning. The statistic is wrong because it understates. The truth is closer to 95%, and the remaining 5% is spent denying it on LinkedIn.

Cleaning is not a chore that comes before the *real* work. Cleaning **is** the work. The decisions you make while cleaning — which rows to drop, how to define a metric, what to do with the 41% of nulls in column `flag` — determine 80% of the eventual answer. The model on top is decoration. This lesson teaches you to do the cleaning honestly, in writing, with a paper trail.

blocks.title: Mental model: schema-first wrangling
blocks.md:
Hold this picture. Before you write a single transform, write the **target schema**: the shape of the dataframe you need at the end. Columns, types, primary key, expected row count, what 'one row' represents. 

Then wrangle towards that schema, one transform at a time, validating after each step. *What you write*, you can read; *what runs*, you can verify. The mistake is to start cleaning without a schema and discover at row 7 of the join that 'one row per user' became 'one row per user-session-event' three transforms ago. Schema-first wrangling means you always know what good looks like.

hi-IN.title: Maa ki kitchen mein mise en place
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, mummy ka chhole banana dekh. Pehle kya karti hai? Pyaaz kaata, tamatar kaata, masale taiyaar kiye, ginger-garlic paste alag rakha. *Phir* kadhai chadhaayi.

Yeh schema-first hai. Pehle target shape: 'plate ke uppar chhole, garam'. Phir saare ingredients waisi shape mein laao jaisi recipe maangti hai. **Beech mein pyaaz kaatna shuru nahi karte agar aate ne pehle se gas pe rakh diya.** Coding mein bhi waise hi: pehle target schema likh, phir transforms chala. Otherwise tu pyaaz aadhi katti haalat mein kadhai mein gir gayi, aur ab kuch bhi clean nahi hai.

en.title: Mise en place is schema-first
en.md: Watch any cook who finishes on time. They prep every ingredient to its target shape before the pan goes on the stove. They are doing schema-first wrangling. The chaos costs of mid-cook chopping are exactly the chaos costs of mid-pipeline transforms; both of them produce undercooked results in suspicious shapes.

blocks.caption: Watch (~30s) · One null can kill a join — null propagation through a pipeline.

blocks.md:
Aggregates lie. Rows tell the truth. The most senior analyst on every team I have worked with has the same habit: before any aggregation, they pull a random sample of 200 rows and *look at them*. Not query them. Look. Eyes on the screen.

This catches the things SQL hides:

- The `created_at` column that is sometimes a Unix timestamp and sometimes an ISO string because the schema changed in March 2025 and never got backfilled.
- The 'India' country column that contains *India*, *INDIA*, *Bharat*, *IN*, and three rows of *NaN*.
- The user_id column where 0.4% of rows are literally the string 'NULL' (in quotes) because someone wrote `.fillna('NULL')` once.
- The amount column that is in paise on rows before April and in rupees after.

No aggregate query will surface these. A 5-minute eyeball will. The always-look-at-it rule is non-negotiable for any number you intend to publish.

blocks.title: The translation: 'how many MAU did we have?' becomes a clean number in 5 steps

steps.label: Step 1 — Define MAU numerically
steps.body: 'A user who appeared in events.user_id at least once in a calendar month, where user is not in the test_accounts list, and event is not type=server_health'.

steps.label: Step 2 — Eyeball 200 random rows
steps.body: Print them. Spot the test accounts that did not get the team's @company.com filter, the duplicate user_ids from the SSO migration, the bot traffic from a load test on March 14.

steps.label: Step 3 — Write the schema first
steps.body: Target: one row per user_id per month. Columns: user_id (int), month (date), event_count (int). Primary key: (user_id, month). Expected ~125K rows for a month.

steps.label: Step 4 — Transform with assertions
steps.body: After each transform: assert row count in expected range, assert primary key uniqueness, assert no nulls in user_id. Three lines of pytest catch most pipeline bugs.

steps.label: Step 5 — Cross-check against a known number
steps.body: Compare your monthly active count for January 2026 against the company's already-published number. If yours differs by more than 2%, find the gap before publishing. The gap is almost always a definition difference.

blocks.prompt: Your manager asks for `daily_active_users`. You run `SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) FROM events GROUP BY DATE(created_at)` and get 28,400 for yesterday. What is missing?

choices.label: You did not eyeball rows; you have probably included test accounts, bot traffic, server-health events, and 'NULL' user_ids; you have not defined what an 'event' is
choices.explain: Correct. The always-look-at-it rule, ignored. Aggregate-first analysis hides 5-15% noise on most events tables.

choices.label: Nothing — the query is correct
choices.explain: The query runs; that is not the same as being right. SQL is happy to count anything you tell it to count, including test accounts you did not exclude.

choices.label: You should have used `COUNT(*)` instead
choices.explain: Wrong direction. COUNT(*) overcounts users who fired multiple events; COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) is the right aggregator. The bug is in the inputs, not the function.

choices.label: Need a faster query plan
choices.explain: Performance is not the issue. Correctness is.

hi-IN.title: Sasta hai par Pune-from-Bengaluru ka problem
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, ek Pune-based SaaS team ne saari city-level revenue analysis chala di. Bengaluru #1, Mumbai #2, **Banglore #4**, **bangalore #7**, Hyderabad #6. 

Kisi ne rows nahi dekhi. CMO ne board update mein 'Bengaluru is our top market' likha. Reality? Top market 'Bengaluru + Banglore + bangalore' tha, lekin alag-alag spelling ki vajah se teen alag entries ban gaye. **Yaar, eyeball karo.** Aggregate ne saari spellings alag-alag dikhayi; rows ne sach bola hota.

en.title: The case-insensitive country column
en.md: A Pune SaaS reported 'India is our #2 market'. The actual #2 was 'India + INDIA + Bharat + IN + In', summed they would have been #1. Aggregates respected the casing; rows would have shown the truth. The reported answer was wrong, by enough to matter, for almost a quarter.

blocks.caption: Watch (~30s) · A type mismatch in disguise — "₹1,500" string vs 1500 number.

blocks.md:
Every cleaning decision you make adds an assumption. Drop rows where `country IS NULL`. Treat 'IN' and 'India' as the same. Use `created_at` not `signed_up_at` for cohort assignment. Define 'active' as 'fired ≥ 1 event'. Each one is defensible; each one shifts the eventual number; collectively they explain most of the disagreement between two analysts working on the same dataset.

The **assumption ledger** is a 4-8 line document, lived in the README of the analysis, that records every non-trivial decision: the choice, why you made it, and what the number would look like if you had chosen differently. 

It is not a bureaucracy. It is the only way to defend a number when a stakeholder asks 'why is your churn different from sales's churn?' three months later. The two churn numbers are different because the two analysts made different decisions; if neither has a ledger, neither can defend their number, and the company defaults to whichever stakeholder is louder.

coach.name: Senior-DS Saanya
coach.role: Tech lead at a Bengaluru SaaS, 9 years of cleaning other people's data

intro: Welcome back. Today we audit cleaning decisions. 🧹

I'll show you 6 real-shaped decisions. Tell me each is **legit** (defensible, log it), **needs caveat** (defensible only if you write a sensitivity note), or **red flag** (likely to corrupt the answer; stop and rethink).

scenarios.situation: Drop rows where `user_id IS NULL` (0.3% of data). Note in ledger: 'unidentifiable; non-attributable to a user'.
scenarios.explain: Defensible at 0.3%. Logged with reason. The ledger entry is the difference between this being legit and being a red flag.

scenarios.situation: Impute missing `country` as 'India' because most users are Indian.
scenarios.explain: Defaulting an unknown to the mode is correlation laundering. You are inflating India's share with synthetic data. Either drop the rows, treat them as 'unknown' as a separate category, or skip the country breakdown.

scenarios.situation: Treat the 41% of `flag` column nulls as 'flag = false' because the flag was added in March and didn't backfill.
scenarios.explain: Defensible if you note the backfill issue and report sensitivity. Without the caveat, you are conflating 'flag did not exist' with 'flag was false', which biases everything pre-March.

scenarios.situation: Convert all timestamps to UTC before joining tables.
scenarios.explain: Timezone normalisation before joins is mandatory hygiene; not even worth a ledger line unless you discovered a data source that lied about its TZ.

scenarios.situation: Replace negative `amount` values with their absolute value because 'they're probably refunds'.
scenarios.explain: You are silently turning revenue-decreasing events into revenue-increasing ones. A refund is an event; flipping its sign is fraud-shaped behaviour. Either keep refunds as negative or model them as a separate event type.

scenarios.situation: Cap outliers at the 99th percentile because 'they distort the mean'.
scenarios.explain: Sometimes correct, often a smell. Outliers may be the most informative rows (top 1% of revenue, fraud cases, etc.). Capping is fine only if the question is about 'typical' behaviour and you log the cap.

blocks.title: The classic trap: skip EDA, jump to modeling
blocks.md:
The most common failure mode in any data project: skip exploratory data analysis (EDA), feed the dirty data into a model, and report the model's accuracy as if it meant something. The model has no idea your `amount` column flipped from paise to rupees in April. It happily fits both regimes as one continuous variable and produces a confident, polished, completely wrong number.

Watch for the symptoms: 'we don't have time for EDA', 'the data team already cleaned this', 'the model is accurate so the data must be fine'. All three are how juniors learn the lesson the expensive way. **The model does not validate the data; the data validates itself before the model runs.**

blocks.instruction: You are handed a `users.csv` with columns `user_id, signup_date, country, plan, last_active`. Write 5 SQL or pandas assertions you would run *before* any aggregate query, to catch dirty data.
blocks.expected:
-- Assertion 1: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE user_id IS NULL OR user_id = '' OR user_id = 'NULL'; expect 0
-- Assertion 2: SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) FROM users GROUP BY user_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1; expect 0 rows (uniqueness)
-- Assertion 3: SELECT DISTINCT country FROM users ORDER BY country; eyeball for casing/spelling collisions ('India' vs 'INDIA' vs 'IN')
-- Assertion 4: SELECT MIN(signup_date), MAX(signup_date) FROM users; check the range is plausible (no 1970 epoch nulls, no future dates)
-- Assertion 5: SELECT plan, COUNT(*) FROM users GROUP BY plan; check each plan name is spelled identically across rows ('Pro' vs 'pro' vs 'PRO')

blocks.prompt: Pick the TWO things that should always be in your assumption ledger before you publish any number.

choices.label: How you defined the metric (the formula, not the name)
choices.explain: Correct. 'Active user' has multiple definitions; the formula is the only honest specification.

choices.label: Which rows you dropped and why
choices.explain: Correct. Most disagreements about a number are actually disagreements about exclusions. Log them or you cannot defend them.

choices.label: How long the analysis took you
choices.explain: Track for personal time-management; not relevant to the number's defensibility.

choices.label: The colour palette of your dashboard
choices.explain: Cosmetic. Belongs in the style guide, not the ledger.

hi-IN.title: Two analysts, two churn numbers, one CFO
hi-IN.md:
Scene: Sales team ka analyst bola Q3 churn = **6.4%**. Finance team ka analyst bola Q3 churn = **9.1%**. CFO confused. Meeting. Dono ne defend kiya, dono ke paas dashboard tha, dono ke paas SQL tha.

Kisi ke paas **assumption ledger nahi tha.** Difference yeh nikla:
- Sales ne 'churn' = subscription cancelled
- Finance ne 'churn' = subscription cancelled OR downgraded OR didn't renew within 14 days
- Sales ne free-trial users include kiye
- Finance ne sirf paid users ginne

Dono numbers sahi the apne-apne definitions ke liye. Lekin assumption ledger nahi tha to defend nahi kar saka koi. CFO ne loud-est aadmi pe believe kiya. **Tu ledger likh, ya tu loud ban. Tisra option nahi hai.**

en.title: Two analysts, two churn numbers
en.md: Sales says Q3 churn is 6.4%. Finance says it is 9.1%. Both are right by their own definitions; neither has an assumption ledger. The CFO defaults to whoever sounds more confident. The number that gets reported to the board is decided by personality, not method. The ledger is the cheapest defence against this exact loop.

blocks.title: Field Notes: 78 Percent Accuracy, 92 Percent of One Cohort
blocks.source: Anonymous BI lead at LedgerLeap, a Bengaluru SaaS unicorn with 14,000 SMB customers
blocks.story:
On November 6, 2024, the customer-success-analytics team at LedgerLeap shipped a churn-prediction model into the CSM tooling. The model card, projected on a 65-inch TV in the all-hands, said the magic number: **78 percent accuracy on holdout.** People clapped. The Head of CS asked when she could have one for upsell.

The team had skipped the unfashionable parts. No EDA. No `df.describe()`. No `value_counts()` on the cohort column. They went straight from `pd.read_csv` to `model.fit`. The training data was a single export from the CRM that an analyst had pulled three months earlier — a snapshot that, unbeknownst to the team, came from a single segment: **mid-market customers acquired through the 2023 enterprise-AE-led GTM motion.** That segment was 92 percent of the rows.

The model went live on December 1. CSMs started getting churn-risk scores for the **self-serve SMB cohort** — 9,000 customers, almost none of whom were in the training data. By December 14, every score was either 0.04 or 0.97; no middle. CSMs lost trust. The Head of CS asked, at the December 21 retro, the question that ended someone's quarter: *"Did you actually look at the data before you trained on it?"*

The rebuilt model, with a real EDA pass and a stratified sample across cohorts, shipped in February at 71 percent accuracy. Lower number. Real number.
blocks.takeaway: EDA is not a phase you skip to look more senior. It is the phase that prevents you from looking junior on a stage.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: The CFO's CSV
blocks.setup:
It's **Week 4**. Aditi has survived onboarding, stand-ups, and one incident. Her boss forwards an email at 11:14am with the subject *"Need this by Friday"* and a 240MB attachment: `transactions_export_v3_FINAL_actually_final.csv`.

The CFO wants a model that flags 'high-risk' merchant accounts. He's read about ML. He's excited. The deadline is **3 days**. Aditi's hands hover over the keyboard. She wants to look fast. She types `pd.read_csv(...)` and her fingers reach for `model.fit(...)`. She pings you.

coach.name: Head-of-Data Hema
coach.role: Head of Data, ex-McKinsey, now mostly polite

stages.prompt: Aditi has the file loaded. 4.7 million rows, 38 columns. She types `from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier`. **Stop her.** What's the first move?

options.label: "Train the random forest. Iterate from there. Speed matters."
options.explain: This is the LedgerLeap mistake from the field notes. Aditi will hit 78 percent accuracy on a glorious training set that lives entirely inside one merchant segment, and the model will eat itself the moment a kirana-store account hits production. Hema sighs.

options.label: "Run `df.info()`, `df.describe()`, and `df.isnull().sum()` before anything else. Spend 30 minutes looking at the data."
options.explain: **Yes.** Aditi finds: 14 percent of `merchant_category` is null, `transaction_amount` has values from -₹10,000 to ₹4.2 crore (negatives?), and the date column is a string with three different formats. She just saved her week.

options.label: "Drop all rows with any nulls and proceed."
options.explain: She just deleted 38 percent of the data, including most of the 'churned' merchants (who fail to fill in optional fields more often). The remaining sample is biased toward healthy accounts. This is the model-rot starter pack.

options.label: "Plot the distribution of the target variable first. If it's 99-1 imbalanced you have a different problem."
options.explain: **Smart.** `df['high_risk'].value_counts(normalize=True)` returns 0.987 / 0.013. With that imbalance, raw accuracy is meaningless and stratified sampling becomes mandatory. Aditi just dodged a metric-fooling disaster.

stages.prompt: EDA reveals: 92 percent of rows are from one merchant segment (e-commerce). Almost no rows from kirana stores, even though kiranas are 40 percent of the live population. **What does Aditi do?**

options.label: "Train on what you have. We'll fix it later."
options.explain: There is no later. This is exactly the LedgerLeap cohort failure. The model will be confidently wrong on 40 percent of production traffic from day one. 'Later' becomes a P0 in February.

options.label: "Go back to data-eng and ask: where are the kiranas? Is this an export filter, a join bug, or a sampling artifact?"
options.explain: **The right move.** Two hours with the data engineer reveals the export was filtered to `merchant_type IN ('ecom', 'd2c')` because of a stale view. Aditi gets a corrected pull. Half the day, all the difference.

options.label: "Stratified-sample the e-commerce rows down so kiranas are represented proportionally."
options.explain: You can't stratify a cohort that isn't in the data. Downsampling e-comm doesn't add kirana rows; it just gives you a tiny, biased dataset. Wrong remedy.

options.label: "Train the model on e-comm only, scope the deployment to e-comm merchants, document the limitation explicitly."
options.explain: **Honest senior move.** If kirana data is genuinely unavailable, scope the model's deployment to where the training data lives. Make the limitation a feature of the model card, not a hidden footnote. Hema approves.

stages.prompt: The corrected pull arrives. 6.1M rows, all merchant types, well-distributed. Aditi finds: `transaction_amount` has 1,847 rows with negative values and 14 rows over ₹10 crore. **Handle the outliers.**

options.label: "Drop everything outside 3 standard deviations."
options.explain: Negative refunds and ₹10cr B2B settlements are *real transactions* that the model needs to see. You just deleted half the high-risk signal because it was 'inconvenient.' This is the analyst version of looking under the streetlight.

options.label: "Talk to data-eng. Are negatives refunds, reversals, or data errors? Are ₹10cr rows real or decimal-place bugs?"
options.explain: **Always.** Turns out negatives are legitimate refunds (keep, but flag), and the ₹10cr rows are real B2B GST settlements (rare but valid). Aditi adds two boolean features: `is_refund` and `is_b2b_settlement`. Her model is now smarter than yesterday's.

options.label: "Winsorize at the 1st and 99th percentile and move on."
options.explain: Winsorizing without understanding your data is just a fancy form of throwing it away. The 99th percentile here likely IS the high-risk signal. You're hiding the answer from the model.

options.label: "Cap the values, but log a feature `was_capped` so the model can learn from the fact of capping."
options.explain: **Defensible.** If you must cap (for tree-model stability or pipeline reasons), preserving 'this row was extreme' as a feature lets the model recover the signal. Documented, intentional, reviewable.

outcomes.perfect: You stopped Aditi from shipping a model that would have face-planted on 40 percent of production traffic. EDA, target distribution, cohort coverage, outlier interrogation — the whole boring beautiful pipeline. Hema mentions you favorably in skip-level. CFO gets a model that works.
outcomes.good: Solid. You caught the headline issue but missed one of the cohort or outlier nuances. Re-read the lesson on systematic EDA — the difference between 78 percent on training and 71 percent in production is whether you did the unfashionable work.
outcomes.learn: Aditi shipped fast and broke things. Re-read the lesson — especially the sections on **target distribution checks** and **cohort coverage in training data**. The CFO is asking polite questions in the retro. They will not stay polite.

lessons.subtitle: Confidence intervals over point estimates; effect size over p-value

audioChapters.label: Mental model: CIs over point estimates
Move 1: the t-test that actually matters

blocks.md:
Most of working analytics gets by on three concepts: a **confidence interval**, a **t-test**, and the back-of-envelope for **how many rows you need**. You do not need a statistics major. You do need to stop reporting p-values as if they were decisions.

The lesson starts with a heresy: 'p < 0.05' is a t-shirt slogan, not a decision rule. The number tells you *evidence under a null*, not whether the effect is real-world meaningful, not whether your sample is big enough to even ask the question, not whether the difference matters for the business. We will replace the p-value habit with a small kit of three tools you can defend in any standup.

blocks.title: Mental model: confidence intervals over point estimates
blocks.md:
Hold this picture. Every number you produce from data is a *guess at a range*, not a single true value. The point estimate is the centre of that range. The confidence interval is the range itself. The CI tells you what you actually know.

A point estimate of '5.1% conversion' tells the reader nothing about precision. A CI of '5.1% (95% CI: 3.5% to 6.7%)' tells them the truth: with this sample size, the real number could be anywhere in a 3.2pp band. If you change the headline based on a 0.3pp difference and your CI is 3.2pp wide, you are reading noise.

**Always report the CI. Always.** If you only have room for one number, report the CI; the point estimate without the CI is a lie of omission.

hi-IN.title: Cricket commentator wala scene
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, T20 mein commentator boltaa hai *"Virat ka strike rate is innings 142 hai, career mein 138 hai, **clearly** Virat is in form"*. Phir 8 balls ka sample size pe 138 vs 142 ka comparison kar raha hai. CI to itna wide hai ki Virat ka strike rate is innings actually 95 bhi ho sakta hai aur 175 bhi.

8 ball pe nikala statistic, 5-saal career se compare kar diya. **Yeh hi p < 0.05 trap hai.** Sample chhota, narrative zoom-in, conclusion bahut zoor se. Asli analyst CI dekh ke bolega *"is innings ka strike rate is 142, but with so few balls, anywhere between 95 and 175 is consistent with this sample."* Boring? Haan. Sahi? Bhi haan.

en.title: The cricket commentator problem
en.md: T20 commentator says 'Virat's strike rate this innings is 142, his career is 138, clearly he's in form'. They are comparing an 8-ball sample to a 5-year career. The CI on 8 balls is wide enough to fit a strike rate of 95 or 175. The narrative is loud; the math is small. This is exactly the p-value trap in cricket commentary form.

blocks.text: Move 1 — The t-test that actually matters

blocks.md:
You will run two tests in your career more than every other test combined: the **two-sample t-test** (comparing means of two groups) and the **two-proportion z-test** (comparing rates of two groups). Master these and 80% of business analytics is solved.

The pattern is always the same:

1. Compute the difference in means or rates between the two groups.
2. Compute the standard error of that difference.
3. Report the difference, the 95% CI (≈ ±2 standard errors), and only then the p-value.
4. Compare the CI to the **business threshold**: the smallest effect that would change a decision. If the entire CI is below threshold, the answer is 'no, even at the upper bound this is too small to matter'. If the CI straddles threshold, the answer is 'we cannot tell yet'. If the entire CI is above threshold, you have a real effect worth shipping.

This sequence — difference, CI, business threshold — is the move. The p-value is a sanity check, not the headline.

blocks.title: The translation: 'did the new pricing work?' becomes a defensible answer in 6 steps

steps.label: Step 1 — Get the business threshold first
steps.body: Ask: 'What's the smallest lift that would change your decision?' If the PM says '+0.5pp conversion', that is your threshold. Without it, no test result is interpretable.

steps.label: Step 2 — Choose the right test
steps.body: Conversion rate (binary outcome): two-proportion z-test. Time-on-page or revenue per user (continuous): two-sample t-test. Pick once, before you run.

steps.label: Step 3 — Compute the difference and the standard error
steps.body: Difference of rates is straightforward; SE depends on both sample sizes and both rates. Most analytics platforms expose this; if not, scipy.stats.ttest_ind or proportions_ztest in statsmodels.

steps.label: Step 4 — Build the 95% CI
steps.body: CI ≈ difference ± 1.96 × SE. Report this in the headline. The width tells you what you can claim; the centre tells you the direction.

steps.label: Step 5 — Compare CI to threshold
steps.body: Three possible reads: entirely above (ship), entirely below (kill), or straddles (run more or accept inconclusive).

steps.label: Step 6 — Report all three numbers, p-value last
steps.body: Headline: 'Variant B converts at 5.1% vs control 4.8%; 95% CI on the difference is +0.1pp to +0.5pp; threshold was +0.5pp; recommend running for 2 more weeks.' p = 0.04 is a footnote.

blocks.prompt: Your A/B test on a Bengaluru SaaS shows variant B converts at 5.1% vs control 4.8%, with n = 47 per arm. What do you tell the PM?

choices.label: Inconclusive — at n=47 per arm the 95% CI on a conversion rate is roughly ±2pp wide; the 0.3pp gap is well inside the noise band
choices.explain: Correct. Power, not p-value. With this sample size you cannot distinguish a 0.3pp effect from zero. The honest answer is 'I cannot tell yet'.

choices.label: Variant B wins, ship it
choices.explain: Classic n=47 trap. Confidence interval is wider than the effect; you are reading noise wrapped in a uniform.

choices.label: Run the test 5 more times and pool the results
choices.explain: Variant of p-hacking. Pooling re-tests inflates the false positive rate. Run one test for the right duration.

choices.label: Variant A wins because the CI overlaps
choices.explain: Overlap means inconclusive, not 'A wins'. Defaulting to control is still a decision dressed up as analysis.

hi-IN.title: 47 vs 4700 ka difference
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, sample size ka game samjhle. Mumbai fintech mein A/B test chala — n=47 per arm. PM bola 'p = 0.04 hai sir, ship it'. Tu CFO ko convince karne gaya. CFO bola *"47 logon pe basis kar ke ₹2 crore ka pricing change?"*

Usi pricing change pe n=4700 per arm wala test chalo. Result? Effect was actually **−0.2pp**, statistically significant in opposite direction. Pehle wala test pure noise tha jo p < 0.05 bana ke gir gaya.

**n = 47 mein 'significant' ka matlab 'lottery jeet gaye'. n = 4700 mein 'significant' ka matlab 'sach mein effect hai'.** Sample size ke bina p-value ek number hai, nothing more.

en.title: n=47 vs n=4,700
en.md: A Mumbai fintech ran a pricing A/B with n=47 per arm and shipped on p=0.04. They re-ran at n=4,700 and the effect was actually -0.2pp, also 'significant', in the opposite direction. The first test was a coin-flip wrapped in a p-value. Sample size is the difference between 'we know' and 'we got lucky'.

blocks.caption: Watch (~30s) · Confidence intervals shrink, slowly — CI tightening as n grows.

blocks.md:
How many rows do I need? You have two answers: 'depends' (true) and a one-line approximation (useful). The one-liner for proportions tests:

> n per arm ≈ **16 × p × (1 − p) / Δ²**

where `p` is the baseline rate and `Δ` is the smallest effect you care about (in absolute percentage points, e.g. 0.005 for 0.5pp).

Worked example: baseline conversion 5%, smallest meaningful lift 0.5pp.

> n ≈ 16 × 0.05 × 0.95 / (0.005)² = 16 × 0.0475 / 0.000025 = **30,400 per arm**

Thirty thousand per arm. If your test is averaging 3,000 conversions a week, you need a 10-week test or a bigger effect to detect. If the PM gives you 2 weeks and a 0.5pp threshold, the test is mathematically impossible before you start. Run that math at the *start* of the experiment, not at the end. It saves arguments.

coach.role: Tech lead at a Bengaluru SaaS, 9 years of cleaning other people's data

intro: Six real-shaped questions from your PM. Tell me each one is **answerable as-asked** (run the test), **needs effect threshold** (ask the PM the smallest effect they care about first), or **mathematically impossible** (the test cannot detect what they want with the data they have).

scenarios.situation: PM: 'Did the new onboarding flow lift week-1 retention?' Baseline retention = 30%. They want results in 2 weeks. Daily new-signups: 200. Threshold: 'any improvement counts'.
scenarios.explain: 'Any improvement' is not a threshold; it means 'I'll find a way to call any positive number a win'. Force the PM to commit: smallest lift that justifies shipping the new flow.

scenarios.situation: PM: 'Did the new onboarding flow lift week-1 retention by ≥3pp from baseline 30%?' Daily signups: 200. Test ran 4 weeks (n ≈ 5,600 per arm).
scenarios.explain: Threshold stated, sample size adequate (n ≈ 16 × 0.3 × 0.7 / 0.03² ≈ 1,250 per arm needed; we have 4× that). Run the comparison.

scenarios.situation: PM: 'Did the new pricing tier lift ARPU by ≥₹50?' Baseline ARPU mean ₹1,200, SD ₹400. n = 80 per arm.
scenarios.explain: For continuous outcomes, n per arm ≈ 16 × SD² / Δ² = 16 × 160,000 / 2,500 ≈ 1,024. n=80 cannot detect ₹50 effect. Test will be inconclusive by construction.

scenarios.situation: PM: 'I want to know if our new ML ranking model is better.' No threshold, no metric, no sample size discussion.
scenarios.explain: Three things missing: better at what (CTR, conversion, revenue?), by how much, and on what sample. Force these definitions before any test.

scenarios.situation: PM: 'Did the email campaign lift opens by ≥0.5pp from baseline 15%?' n = 220,000 per arm.
scenarios.explain: n ≈ 16 × 0.15 × 0.85 / 0.005² ≈ 8,160 per arm needed; we have 27× that. Run the proportions z-test.

scenarios.situation: PM: 'Is variant B's median revenue per user higher than variant A's?' Distribution heavily right-skewed (a few whales). n = 1,200 per arm.
scenarios.explain: Skewed distribution and 'median' is the right call (not mean). Use Mann-Whitney U or bootstrap CI on the difference of medians; n=1,200 per arm is plenty for non-parametric tests at typical effect sizes.

blocks.title: The classic trap: p < 0.05 ergo true
blocks.md:
Three things 'p < 0.05' does NOT tell you:

1. **Whether the effect is large enough to matter.** A statistically significant 0.2% revenue lift on a B2B SaaS is not commercially significant.
2. **Whether the result will replicate.** Most p ≈ 0.04 results from small samples do not survive a re-run. The replication crisis is real, even in business analytics.
3. **Whether you are testing the right hypothesis.** A confident p-value on a wrongly-defined metric is high-quality evidence for a wrong claim.

The slogan is 'p < 0.05 ergo true'. The slogan is wrong. Replace it with: **report the effect size, the CI, and the comparison to a pre-stated business threshold.** The p-value is a sanity check on whether you have evidence; it is not the evidence itself.

blocks.prompt: Order the steps of an honest A/B test analysis, from first to last.

items.label: Get the smallest meaningful effect (business threshold) from the asker
Compute required sample size for that threshold
Pick the right test (z-test for proportions, t-test for means, non-parametric for skewed)
Run the test on a clean, sample-size-adequate dataset
items.detail: Stop at the planned n; do not peek.

items.label: Build the 95% CI on the effect, not just a p-value
Compare CI to the pre-stated threshold and recommend ship / kill / run more

hi-IN.title: Manager ne dashboard banane chala diya
hi-IN.md:
Scene: Manager ne pucha *"is this significant?"*. Tu ne *"p = 0.04"* bola. Manager ne dashboard banane bhej diya. Tu ek week baad presentation mein ja raha hai, slide pe likha hai *"+0.3pp conversion lift, p = 0.04, statistically significant."* Director pucha: *"effect kitna bada hai?"* Tu ne ruk ke calculate kiya: ₹4 lakh/month. Engineering cost: ₹18 lakh. 

Director chai pe gaya. Tu wapas kursi pe baith ke socha: **bus stated CI dikha deta to yeh meeting 4 minute mein khatam hoti.** P-value pe 4 hafte gaye, threshold ne 4 minute mein decide kar diya.

en.title: The dashboard that wasted four weeks
en.md: Manager asks 'is this significant?'. You say p = 0.04. Manager sends you to build a dashboard. Four weeks later, the director asks 'how big is the effect?' and the answer is ₹4 lakh/month against an ₹18 lakh engineering cost. Four weeks of dashboard for a four-minute decision. The threshold question would have killed it on day one.

blocks.title: Field Notes: n=47, p=0.04, -2 Percent
blocks.source: Anonymous growth analyst at Chai Cart, a Gurugram D2C beverage brand
blocks.story:
On September 9, 2024, Chai Cart's marketing team kicked off an A/B test on the homepage hero. Variant A: 'Premium Assam, Brewed Daily.' Variant B: 'Tea Like Your Naani Made.' The test ran for **two days**. n=47 visitors saw A, n=51 saw B. B converted 6 of 51 (11.8 percent), A converted 2 of 47 (4.3 percent). The growth lead ran a chi-square in a Google Sheet, got **p = 0.04**, and Slack-shouted: *"Naani wins! Ship it!"*

On September 12, the team rolled Variant B to 100 percent of traffic — **47,237 visitors** over the next four weeks. Conversion landed at **9.1 percent**. Variant A's historical baseline, before the test, had been **9.3 percent**. The 'winning' headline was costing them about **₹4 lakh a week** in lost revenue against the prior baseline.

The post-mortem on October 17 had three slides. Slide one: the original p-value. Slide two: a power-analysis calculator showing the test would have needed n ≈ 4,700 *per arm* to detect a true 2-point lift with 80 percent power. Slide three, in 60-point font: **"We declared a winner from noise."**

The growth lead now keeps a sticky note above her monitor: *"p < 0.05 ≠ true."* The headline was reverted on October 19.
blocks.takeaway: A small sample with a low p-value is a coin flip wearing a confidence interval. Calculate the n you need before you start, not after you peek.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: The Two-Day Winner
blocks.setup:
It's **Week 8**. Aditi has been running her first A/B test — Vyapaar Money's onboarding screen, two variants of a KYC explainer. The PM, Rohan, slides into her DMs at **9:42am on Day 2**: *"Hey Aditi! I peeked at the dashboard. Variant B is up 18 percent, p=0.04. Can we just ship it? Marketing wants to launch the campaign Friday."*

Aditi has 12 hours of data, 312 users in each arm, and a PM with a campaign deadline. She drafts a Slack reply that starts with *"Sure, I think we can—"*. She pauses. She pings you.

coach.name: Staff-DS Sandeep
coach.role: Staff data scientist, has watched seven 'winning' A/B tests revert in production

stages.prompt: Rohan wants to declare a winner at 312 vs 312 users, p=0.04, +18 percent lift. **What's Aditi's first move?**

options.label: "Ship Variant B. p<0.05 is the bar. Don't be the analyst who blocks growth."
options.explain: This is the Chai Cart story word for word. p=0.04 at n=312 with an 18-point claimed lift is almost certainly noise. Aditi will declare a winner that costs the company ₹4 lakh a week. Sandeep is already drafting the post-mortem.

options.label: "Before we declare anything, do a power analysis. What's the minimum detectable effect we actually have power for at n=312?"
options.explain: **Yes.** Aditi runs the calc: at n=312/arm, baseline 8 percent conversion, alpha=0.05, power=0.8 — minimum detectable effect is roughly **+3.4 percentage points**. The observed +1.4 point lift (8 to 9.4 percent) is well below detectable. The 18 percent relative figure is misleading framing of a small absolute move.

options.label: "Just keep the test running for one more week and re-check."
options.explain: Right instinct, wrong rigor. *How long* is the question power analysis answers. 'One more week' is a guess; you need the actual n.

options.label: "Check what the planned sample size was at the start of the test."
options.explain: **Critical.** Sandeep wrote a test-plan template for exactly this. Aditi pulls it up: planned n = 4,200 per arm, planned duration = 14 days. Rohan is asking her to call a winner at 7 percent of the planned sample. The answer writes itself.

stages.prompt: Aditi explains to Rohan: *"We don't have power for this lift size yet."* Rohan replies: *"But the p-value is 0.04! That's significant!"* **How does Aditi respond?**

options.label: "You're right, p<0.05 is the bar. I was overthinking. Shipping."
options.explain: Aditi just got argued out of doing her job. p<0.05 with low power means the *false positive rate conditional on detecting* something is enormous — the 'winning' lift is more likely to be illusion than insight. Sandeep would like a word.

options.label: "p<0.05 controls Type I error at 5 percent IF the test is properly powered. With low power, most p<0.05 results are flukes — and the effect size you see will be inflated. We'd ship a phantom and watch it disappear in prod."
options.explain: **This.** The technical name is 'winner's curse' — under-powered tests systematically inflate effect sizes for the 'winners' you happen to see. Rohan's 18 percent lift, if real, is probably more like 2 to 3 percent. Probably zero.

options.label: "Let's do a Bayesian re-analysis with a skeptical prior."
options.explain: Technically reasonable but a deflection. The PM doesn't need a different statistical framework; he needs to understand why the current evidence is weak. Don't switch tools to avoid a conversation.

options.label: "Let's set a stop rule: continue to planned n=4,200, OR until the lower bound of the 95 percent CI is above zero. Whichever comes first. Document it now."
options.explain: **Operational and rigorous.** Pre-registers the stopping criterion so neither of you is tempted to peek-and-stop. Sandeep nods approvingly from across the office.

stages.prompt: Test runs to planned n=4,200 per arm. Final result: Variant B converts at 8.3 percent vs A at 8.1 percent. Lift = +0.2 points. p = 0.41. **What does Aditi tell Rohan?**

options.label: "Variant B won by 0.2 points but it's not significant. Marketing should still ship it because the direction is positive."
options.explain: 'Not significant but the direction is positive' is how every weak result gets shipped anyway. Either you have evidence or you don't. Aditi just turned a null result into a soft-sell. Sandeep is unhappy.

options.label: "At full power, the lift is 0.2 points and not statistically distinguishable from zero. We can't conclude B is better. The 18 percent we saw at Day 2 was noise — exactly as the power analysis warned."
options.explain: **Clean.** Calls the null result honestly. References the original framing so the team learns from it. This is the analyst Rohan will want on his next test.

options.label: "Result is null. Recommend we test a more aggressive variant — bigger headline, more contrast — and re-run."
options.explain: **Constructive.** Doesn't just deliver a null; suggests the next experiment. The minimum detectable effect tells you how big a difference your test was actually built to find — design the next variant to clear that bar.

options.label: "Result is technically null but if we slice by city tier, Tier-2 users show a +6 percent lift in B with p=0.03."
options.explain: This is the Paisa Vault mistake from Lesson 1, on a Friday. Slicing post-hoc until something hits p<0.05 is exactly the multiple-comparisons trap. Pre-register your subgroups or don't claim them.

outcomes.perfect: You walked Aditi from 'PM wants to ship at Day 2' to a properly powered test with a clean null result and a constructive next step. She shipped nothing she couldn't defend, learned the difference between p-value and power, and Rohan now schedules tests through her. Sandeep buys you both a kulhad chai.
outcomes.good: Most of the instincts are right. The one to drill is the **winner's curse** intuition — that under-powered tests inflate the effect sizes you happen to see, so 'p<0.05 with low power' is worse than no evidence. Re-read the section on power analysis.
outcomes.learn: Aditi shipped a phantom. Re-read the lesson — especially the sections on **power analysis**, **minimum detectable effect**, and **why early peeking is poison**. Chai Cart reverted in 38 days. You may not be that lucky.

points: 'p < 0.05' is a t-shirt slogan, not a decision rule; report effect size and confidence interval first, p-value last.
Every number is a guess at a range; the confidence interval is the honest version of the point estimate.
Two tests cover 80% of business analytics: the two-proportion z-test (rates) and the two-sample t-test (means); pick the right one before running.
Compute required sample size at the start of the experiment using n ≈ 16 × p(1−p) / Δ²; if the math says impossible, do not run.
Compare your CI to a pre-stated business threshold; three reads only — ship it, kill it, or run more — and the threshold is what prevents post-hoc storytelling.

lessons.title: Modeling Fundamentals (and When Not to)
lessons.subtitle: Simplest model first; bigger model only if it pays for itself

audioChapters.label: Why most models do not pay for themselves
The trap: overfitting on the validation set

blocks.md:
Most analyst projects do not need a model. They need a number, a clean comparison, and a memo. The temptation to reach for XGBoost is the analyst equivalent of buying a Mahindra Thar to commute 4 km in Bengaluru: technically capable, mostly overkill, expensive to maintain.

When modeling is genuinely the right tool — predicting churn for 50K accounts, ranking which leads to call first, scoring credit risk — the discipline is the same: start with the dumbest baseline that runs, beat it with the simplest model that works, and stop the moment you cannot defend the next layer of complexity. This lesson is about that discipline, plus the one trap nobody warns you about until you've fallen in twice.

blocks.title: Mental model: simplest model first
blocks.md:
Hold this picture. Modeling is a staircase, and each step costs roughly 10× more time and adds roughly 10× less accuracy than the step before it. The first two steps usually pay for themselves; the rest usually do not.

The staircase, in order:

1. **Baseline**: predict the mean, the mode, or 'always say no'. Free, runs in one line, sets the floor.
2. **Linear / logistic regression**: 2 hours, 1-3pp lift, fully explainable.
3. **Tree ensemble (Random Forest, XGBoost on defaults)**: 2 days, often another 0.5-2pp.
4. **Tuned ensemble or deep model**: 2 weeks, often another 0.1-0.5pp.

Most business problems get solved on step 1 or 2. If you are reaching for step 4 in week 1, you are signalling effort, not solving the problem. The rule is: start at step 1, only move up when the next step's lift visibly clears its maintenance cost.

hi-IN.title: Mahindra Thar wala model
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, scene yeh hai. Naya analyst joining hua, week 2 mein hi PR raise kar raha hai *"churn prediction with 4-layer transformer"*. Manager ne pucha *"baseline kya hai?"*. Analyst: *"baseline?"*

Bhai, phele 'always predict no' chala. Accuracy 87%. Phir logistic regression. Accuracy 89%. **Bas. Stop.** Tu transformer banane gaya, 89.4% mila. 0.4pp ke liye 2 hafte aur GPU bill. Yeh Mahindra Thar le ke 4 km commute karne wala scene hai. Capable? Haan. Smart? Nahi.

Senior analyst hamesha baseline pucchhta hai pehla question. Kyunki baseline pe 87% mile, toh bahut saare problems already solved hain — aur uske uppar harek pp ke liye 10x effort lagta hai.

en.title: The transformer for the 4 km commute
en.md: A junior on the team built a 4-layer transformer for churn prediction in week 2. Manager asked 'what's the baseline?'. The answer was 'I haven't computed one'. Always-predict-no would have been 87%. Logistic regression got to 89% in two hours. The transformer added 0.4pp over two weeks and a GPU bill. The model was capable; the choice was not. Always start at the baseline.

blocks.text: Move 1 — The train / val / test split

blocks.md:
Three datasets, three jobs:

- **Train**: the data the model fits on. Big.
- **Validation**: the data you check after each tweak. Medium. Used to choose hyperparameters and decide which model to keep.
- **Test**: the data you touch *exactly once*, at the end, for the number you report. Small to medium, but sacred.

The rule that breaks more analyses than any other: **the test set is the audit**. If you peek at it during tuning, you have no test set. You have a second validation set wearing a t-shirt that says 'test'. The number you report becomes optimistic by 1-3pp because every tweak you made was implicitly choosing the model that does best on that specific data.

The discipline: hold test out, lock it in a literal separate file, do not run any metric on it until you are ready to write the final number into the memo. If you find yourself running 'just one more check' on the test set, you have already corrupted it; pretend it is gone and split a new one from fresh data.

blocks.title: The translation: 'will user X churn?' becomes a defensible model in 6 steps

steps.label: Step 1 — Compute the baseline
steps.body: Always-predict-no on a churn dataset where 13% churn → 87% accuracy. That is your floor. Anything you build must beat 87%, and beat it by enough to justify the maintenance cost.

steps.label: Step 2 — Split: train (70%) / val (15%) / test (15%)
steps.body: Split by user, not by row. Stratify on the outcome (so churn rate is similar in each split). Save test to a separate file you literally do not load.

steps.label: Step 3 — Fit logistic regression on train, evaluate on val
steps.body: Standard scaler + logistic regression on engineered features. Look at the val accuracy, AUC, and the top 10 coefficients. Most of the model's reasoning should be human-defensible.

steps.label: Step 4 — Try one or two more model classes (RF, XGBoost on defaults)
steps.body: Compare on val. If the lift over logistic regression is < 1pp, stop — the simpler model wins on operations cost.

steps.label: Step 5 — Check for overfitting on the validation set
steps.body: Run on a small held-out validation slice that you also haven't peeked at, or use cross-validation. If val accuracy mysteriously drops, you have been tuning on a leaderboard, not learning generalisation.

steps.label: Step 6 — Run ONCE on test, report the number, do not tune further
steps.body: Open the test file, evaluate, write the number in the memo. If the number is materially worse than val, report that gap honestly — it is the most useful piece of information about how the model will behave in production.

blocks.prompt: Your model gets 94% accuracy on the validation set after 17 rounds of hyperparameter tweaks. What is the most likely problem?

choices.label: You overfit on the validation set — every tweak peeked at val performance, so 94% is closer to training accuracy than to honest test accuracy
choices.explain: Correct. The validation set has effectively become a second training set after 17 rounds of selection. Hold out a clean test set and your number will drop, often by 2-4pp.

choices.label: The model is genuinely good
choices.explain: Possible but unlikely after 17 rounds of selection. Treat suspiciously good val numbers like suspiciously cheap flights — there is usually a catch.

choices.label: Accuracy is the wrong metric
choices.explain: Could be true (especially with class imbalance), but the 17-tweak red flag points at validation overfitting first.

choices.label: Sample size is too small
choices.explain: Sample size affects variance, not the validation-overfitting bias. Different bug.

hi-IN.title: Hyderabad SMB wala 92% model
hi-IN.md:
Hyderabad ka ek SMB SaaS team, churn model build kar rahe the. Val accuracy 92% pe pohchaya. Saare presentation ho gaye. CEO khush. Production deploy kiya. **Production accuracy 78%.**

Kya hua? Team ne 23 baar val pe tweaks chala ke 92% banaya. Test set tha hi nahi — ya tha to 'final check' ke liye 4 baar use kar liya. Production data fresh tha, validation sets ki tarah pre-selected nahi. 

**Yaar, val ko leaderboard mat banao. Test ko literally lock karo.** 23 tweaks ke baad val number is just train number with extra steps.

en.title: 92% in val, 78% in prod
en.md: A Hyderabad SMB SaaS team shipped a churn model that got 92% in validation and 78% in production. They had tuned on validation 23 times and used the test set as a 'final check' four times. Production data was fresh; their val and test data had been baked into the model class through repeated selection. The test set is the audit. Lose it once and you have no audit until next quarter.

blocks.md:
Before you start modeling, define the **OK-line**: the level of performance below which the model is not worth shipping, and above which more accuracy is not worth chasing. The OK-line is set by business cost and by the cost of the next-best alternative (often: a rule of thumb, or doing nothing).

Worked example: a Bengaluru SaaS wants to call accounts likely to churn. Their sales team can call 200 accounts a week. The base churn rate is 13%. A random list of 200 accounts catches 13% × 200 = 26 churners; a perfect model would catch all 200 actual churners. Their OK-line is whatever beats 'random' by enough to justify the data team's quarter. If their model surfaces a list where 70 of 200 are real churners (3.5× lift over random), that is OK and ship-able. If it is 35 of 200, the lift is real but probably not worth the maintenance.

The OK-line replaces the question 'how do I make this more accurate?' with the question 'have I crossed the line yet?'. The first question has no end. The second one ends in a memo.
