coach.role: Tech lead at a Bengaluru SaaS, 9 years of cleaning other people's data

intro: Six modeling decisions from your week. Tell me each is **good move** (start here), **second-best** (will work but you skipped a cheaper option), or **stop and step back** (you are solving the wrong problem).

scenarios.situation: Stakeholder asks for churn prediction. You compute the always-predict-no baseline as your first commit.
scenarios.explain: Always start at the baseline. Sets the floor and frames every later model's lift in honest terms.

scenarios.situation: Same stakeholder. You start with a 4-layer LSTM in week 1.
scenarios.explain: Skipping logistic regression and tree ensembles. You will get an accurate-looking model you cannot defend, cannot maintain, and probably overfit the validation set on.

scenarios.situation: Your val accuracy is 89% after 4 small tweaks. Test accuracy when you finally check it: 88.6%. You report 88.6%.
scenarios.explain: Honest. Small val/test gap (4 tweaks is a normal amount). The discipline of running test once and reporting is the gold standard.

scenarios.situation: You retrain a logistic regression on the full dataset (train+val+test) before deploying because 'more data is always better'.
scenarios.explain: Acceptable practice if (a) you have already locked in the test number for reporting and (b) you re-evaluate against fresh held-out data in production. Dangerous if used to chase a higher reported number.

scenarios.situation: Your random forest gets 89% and your XGBoost gets 89.5%. You ship XGBoost.
scenarios.explain: The 0.5pp lift may not pay for the maintenance cost of an XGBoost model in production (more deps, more tuning, harder explainability). The right call depends on cost; ship RF unless you have evidence the 0.5pp matters.

scenarios.situation: You re-run hyperparameter search 12 times against the test set to push reported accuracy up.
scenarios.explain: Test set has been corrupted. The number you eventually report is overfit on test. Either split a fresh test set from new data or report the val number with a 'no clean test held' caveat.

blocks.caption: Watch the trap happen live — and the fix at the end.

blocks.title: The classic trap: overfitting on the validation set
blocks.md:
Most analysts know not to peek at the test set. Almost no analyst notices when they are *overfitting on the validation set* — and that is the trap that quietly poisons production models.

The symptom: you have run 15-25 rounds of hyperparameter tuning, model selection, feature engineering, all evaluated on val. Each round picks the variant that does best on val. After 20 rounds, the variant you keep is the one whose noise pattern happens to align with val's noise pattern. Your val number is now optimistic by 1-3pp.

The fixes are unglamorous: limit yourself to a small number of distinct model variants (5-10, not 50), use cross-validation rather than a single val split, and most importantly **set a tweak budget at the start** — e.g. 'I will stop iterating after 10 evaluations on val, regardless of where I am'. The discipline is to stop, not to iterate further. The model you ship at iteration 10 is, on average, better in production than the one you ship at iteration 30.

blocks.instruction: A PM asks: 'we want to predict which of our 50,000 active accounts will churn next month so sales can call them. Sales can call 500/week. Base churn rate is 9%. What's the OK-line and how would you defend it?'
blocks.starter:
Random baseline (calling 500 random accounts catches): 
OK-line (lift over random worth shipping): 
Why: 
What to report alongside accuracy:
blocks.expected:
Random baseline (calling 500 random accounts catches): 9% × 500 = 45 actual churners
OK-line (lift over random worth shipping): at minimum 2× lift = ~90 churners in the top 500, ideally 3×+ = ~135 churners
Why: 2× lift roughly doubles sales effectiveness, justifies the model's quarter of build + maintenance. Below 2× and you might as well let sales pick by gut.
What to report alongside accuracy: precision@500 (how many of the top 500 ranked are real churners), recall@500 (what % of all churners are in the top 500), lift over random, and the val/test gap so the PM knows how much production drift to expect.

blocks.prompt: Pick the TWO things that should always go in a modeling memo before the accuracy number.

choices.label: The baseline performance (random / always-predict-mode / rule-of-thumb) so the model's lift is interpretable
choices.explain: Correct. 89% accuracy is meaningless without knowing whether baseline was 50% or 87%. Every memo opens with the baseline.

choices.label: The OK-line (the level of performance that justifies shipping vs not)
choices.explain: Correct. Without an OK-line, every accuracy number is open-ended ('but could it be higher?'). With one, you have a binary decision.

choices.label: The number of GPU hours used
choices.explain: Vanity metric. Belongs in cost reporting, not in the modeling memo headline.

choices.label: Which IDE you used
choices.explain: Genuinely irrelevant.

hi-IN.title: Boolean rule beats LSTM
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, ek Mumbai fintech ne 6 mahine LSTM model build kara fraud detection ke liye. Final accuracy: 91%. 

Fraud team ka senior CFO uncle ne Excel kholke 3 boolean rules likhi: *amount > ₹50,000 AND new_account AND foreign_IP*. Accuracy on the same data: 89%. **6 mahine ka LSTM 2pp jeeta, 89% lift over 3 lines of Excel.**

Maintenance cost? LSTM = 1 ML engineer 25% time + GPU bill + retraining. Excel = aunty checks once a month. 

**Simplest model first ka matlab yeh nahi hai 'fancy mat banaao'. Iska matlab hai 'pehle dumb wala chala, dekh kya beat karna hai, phir socho fancy chahiye bhi ya nahi'.**

en.title: Three boolean rules vs the LSTM
en.md: A Mumbai fintech spent six months training an LSTM for fraud detection. Final accuracy 91%. The fraud team's CFO wrote three boolean rules in Excel that hit 89%. The LSTM beat the Excel by 2pp; the Excel beat the LSTM by six months and an entire ML engineer's quarter. Always start at the baseline. The dumb thing is often the right thing.

blocks.title: Field Notes: 94 Percent on Validation, 71 Percent on Reality
blocks.source: Anonymous senior data scientist at Khaata Capital, a Mumbai-based credit-risk NBFC
blocks.story:
Through October and November of 2024, the credit-risk modelling team at Khaata Capital ran what they called the *"Q4 Sprint."* The goal: a new default-prediction model for the salaried-personal-loan book, replacing a tired logistic regression that had been in prod since 2022. The sprint brief was a single line on a whiteboard: *"Highest validation accuracy wins."*

Over six weeks, the team trained **47 model variants**. XGBoost with 12 different hyperparameter grids. LightGBM. CatBoost. A Keras MLP someone had clearly built on a Saturday. They evaluated each variant on the same 20 percent validation slice, picked the leaderboard winner — an XGBoost ensemble at **94.1 percent validation accuracy** — and shipped it on December 18 in time for the year-end push.

The model was deployed against an unseen holdout test set on January 9, 2025, as part of a routine model-risk-management audit that the team had treated as a formality. **Test accuracy: 71.3 percent.** Worse than the 2022 baseline. The 23-point gap was the cleanest case of validation overfitting the audit committee had seen in three years.

What happened: every hyperparameter choice, every feature-engineering decision, every "let's try one more variant" iteration had been made by checking the validation set. With 47 variants, the validation set had effectively become a second training set — and the team had memorised it. The honest test set, untouched until January, told the truth.

The fix took eight weeks. The new modelling protocol now requires a sealed test set, opened once, by the audit lead. The model that finally shipped scored 76 percent on test. Lower than the leaderboard. Real.
blocks.takeaway: If you check it, you've trained on it. The test set is sacred or it is useless.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: The 94 Percent Model
blocks.setup:
It's **Week 14**. Aditi has built her first real model — a fraud-flag classifier on Vyapaar Money's UPI transactions. She's been at it for three weeks. Her latest XGBoost variant, after some careful feature engineering and roughly 30 hyperparameter trials, scores **94.2 percent on validation.** She's elated. She's also two days from the demo to the Risk team.

She Slacks her boss: *"Model is at 94 percent val accuracy. Should I write up the demo deck?"* Boss replies, *"Great! Get it ready."* She opens the deck template. She pings you, half-asking, half-bragging.

coach.name: Head-of-Data Hema
coach.role: Head of Data, owns the model-risk-management framework, has read every Khaata-style audit

stages.prompt: Aditi shares the results: 94.2 percent on val, achieved after 30 hyperparameter trials and 6 feature-engineering iterations, all evaluated on the **same validation slice**. **What do you tell her?**

options.label: "94 percent is great. Demo the deck. Risk will love it."
options.explain: Hema reads this in the audit. Aditi just walked the Khaata Capital playbook from the field notes. The 94 percent is a leaderboard score on a validation set that's been peeked at 30+ times. It is a memorisation artifact, not a generalisation estimate.

options.label: "You've effectively trained on the validation set with 30 trials. Before the demo, hold out a fresh test set you haven't touched, evaluate once, and report THAT number."
options.explain: **Yes.** Repeated validation evaluation is implicit training. The honest evaluation requires data the model and the modeller have never seen. Aditi pulls a clean January-February holdout that wasn't part of the original split. One evaluation. No peeking.

options.label: "Run cross-validation on the 30 best models and report the mean."
options.explain: CV on the same data you've been tuning against doesn't fix the leak — it just averages it. The fundamental issue is that the validation set has been a feedback signal for 30 decisions. Averaging the leak is still leaking.

options.label: "What was the validation score of the FIRST model you tried, before any tuning? If it was much lower than 94, that's a tell."
options.explain: **Sharp.** Aditi checks: first model scored 81 percent on val. After 30 trials, 94 percent. A 13-point climb on the same slice without architectural changes is the signature of validation overfitting. The number itself is a red flag.

stages.prompt: Aditi pulls a fresh January-February holdout test set. Evaluates the 94 percent model **once**. Test accuracy: **76.4 percent.** She panics. *"I have to demo in 36 hours and my real number is 18 points lower than what I thought."* **What's the move?**

options.label: "Re-tune on the new test set until you get back to 94. Demo that."
options.explain: Hema would in fact resign over this. Re-tuning on the test set is the entire failure mode the test set exists to prevent. Aditi would now have *two* contaminated datasets and zero honest signal. This is a fireable mistake at a regulated NBFC.

options.label: "Demo the 76.4 percent number. Frame the 94-vs-76 gap as a finding about the modelling process and what you've learned."
options.explain: **Bold and correct.** Senior people will respect honest 76 over fake 94 every time. Hema has watched a dozen analysts try to fudge the number and exactly one analyst lead with it. That one is now a Director.

options.label: "Cancel the demo, ask for two more weeks to do it properly."
options.explain: This is anxiety masquerading as rigor. The demo is a checkpoint, not a launch. Use it to share the real state. Postponing because the number isn't pretty is how analysts get a reputation for over-promising.

options.label: "Investigate the gap: which segments degrade most? Is it temporal drift, feature leakage in training, or generalisation failure?"
options.explain: **The diagnostic move.** A 18-point gap usually points to *something specific* — often a feature that leaked future information, or a cohort shift between train and test. Aditi finds: a `last_30d_chargeback_count` feature was computed using the WHOLE dataset including future months. Patches it. Re-evaluates. Real number lands at 79 percent. That she can demo with pride.

stages.prompt: Demo day. Aditi has a real test number (79.1 percent), a clean test protocol, and a story about how she found and fixed the leak. The Risk Director asks: **"What's your protocol going forward to make sure this doesn't happen on the next model?"** What does she say?

options.label: "I'll be more careful next time."
options.explain: Process failures need process fixes, not promises. 'Be more careful' is what every analyst says before the next overfit. The Risk Director writes a small note in their pad.

options.label: "Sealed test set, opened once by an independent reviewer, only after the model is finalised. Pre-registered evaluation criteria. Validation set used for tuning, but tuning budget capped at 20 trials with documented hyperparameters."
options.explain: **Audit-grade.** This is roughly the protocol Khaata Capital adopted post-failure. Sealed test, independent open, pre-registered metrics, capped tuning budget. The Risk Director nods and asks her to write it up as the team standard.

options.label: "Switch to nested cross-validation and report mean +/- std."
options.explain: Nested CV is a useful tool but not a substitute for a held-out test set in a regulated environment. Auditors want evidence that the model has been evaluated on data the modeller has never touched. Means and stds don't replace that.

options.label: "Build a second model, completely independently, and require both to agree before flagging a transaction."
options.explain: Different problem. Ensembling is about robustness; the question was about evaluation discipline. Strong-sounding but doesn't address what was asked.

outcomes.perfect: You stopped Aditi from demoing a fairy-tale 94 percent, helped her find a real 79 percent (with a leak fix), and walked her through articulating an audit-grade evaluation protocol. Hema mentions this in the all-hands as 'how we want every model demo to go from now on.' That's a career-bending day.
outcomes.good: Solid on the headline issues. The protocol-design step is where the senior signal lives — re-read the section on **sealed test sets and pre-registered evaluation**. Numbers are easy to fake; processes are what auditors trust.
outcomes.learn: Aditi demoed 94 percent, the number didn't survive Risk's holdout audit on Monday morning, and the model never shipped. Re-read the lesson — especially the sections on **validation overfitting**, **the once-and-only-once test set**, and **how 47 trials becomes 47 ways to memorise the val slice**.

blocks.caption: Try (~60s) · When would NOT modeling be smarter? — pick the scenario where a model is overkill.

points: Most analyst questions do not need a model; they need a clean comparison and a memo. Reach for a model only when ranking or scoring at scale is genuinely the job.
The modeling staircase is logarithmic in cost: each step costs roughly 10× more and adds roughly 10× less than the step before it.
Train, val, test — and the test set is the audit; touch it once, at the end, or you have no test set.
Overfitting on the validation set is the trap nobody warns you about; cap your tweaks at 5-10 distinct variants and stop on schedule.
Define the OK-line at the start; the question is 'have I crossed it?', not 'how high can I go?'.

blocks.prompt: Pick the last model you built or wanted to build. Did you compute the baseline before fitting? Did you set an OK-line? Could you tell me, right now, the gap between your val and test numbers, and how many distinct hyperparameter variants you tried? If any answer is 'no' or 'I don't know', that gap is the lesson.

audioChapters.label: Why most data memos die unread
The trap: ship the model, not the story

blocks.md:
Most analysis dies in the inbox. Twenty-eight slides, six tabs, three regression tables, no answer in the first paragraph. The CFO scrolls, scrolls, gives up, defaults to whatever the loudest VP said in standup. Your six weeks of work just made the weather.

The problem is not the analysis. The problem is the artifact. Stakeholders do not read the way analysts write — they scan headlines, they want the answer in sentence one, they decide in 90 seconds whether to keep reading. This lesson is the discipline of producing artifacts that survive that 90 seconds.

blocks.title: Mental model: BLUF — bottom-line up front
blocks.md:
Hold this picture. Every memo, slide, Slack message, email opens with the answer. Not the agenda. Not the methodology. Not the caveats. The answer.

The military invented BLUF for a reason: when stakes are high and time is short, you do not bury the lead. The first sentence should answer the question that was asked. The second sentence should say what to do about it. The third sentence should hint at how confident you are. Everything else — methodology, sample sizes, regression coefficients, the part where you're proud of how clever the join was — goes below the fold.

The rule: if your reader stops at sentence one, they should still be able to act.

blocks.caption: Watch a 28-slide deck collapse into a one-page BLUF memo. Notice what gets kept, what becomes appendix, what disappears entirely.

hi-IN.title: WhatsApp forward wala scene
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, mummy ka WhatsApp forward dekh. Pura paragraph. *"Aaj subah uth ke socha ki tum sab ke liye kuch likhna chahiye, kyunki kal raat tumhare papa ne kaha tha..."* — 14 lines mein actual message ek line ki hai: *"Sunday lunch ke liye 12 baje aana."*

Analyst memos bhi same. Method, methodology, scope, caveats, 8 slides, phir actual answer slide 11 pe. **Mummy ki forward ko BLUF mein convert karo:** *"Sunday lunch 12 baje. Saari details neeche."* Done. Pura WhatsApp empire change ho jaaye.

en.title: The fourteen-line WhatsApp forward
en.md: Mothers worldwide write the WhatsApp forward in the worst possible structure: 14 lines of context to a one-line ask. Analyst memos are the same disease in different clothes. The fix is the same: lead with the ask, attach the context. If the reader can act on sentence one, the rest is bonus.

blocks.caption: Watch (~30s) · Same data, three different talks — one chart, three audiences.

blocks.md:
Every memo gets exactly **one chart that proves the headline**. One. The BLUF chart's job is to make the conclusion visually obvious in 5 seconds. Everything else is appendix.

The BLUF chart is not the most beautiful chart you produced. It is the chart whose visual gestalt matches the sentence in the headline. If the headline is 'churn rose driven by Tier B', the chart shows churn over time, with Tier B highlighted, with a vertical line at the inflection point. The reader does not have to read axis labels to *get it*. Their eye does the work.

Two design rules that catch most analysts:

- **Highlight what you mean, not everything you have.** The chart has the conclusion in colour and the rest in grey. If five lines are equally bright, the reader does not know which one is the point.
- **Annotate.** A short label on the chart pointing at the relevant feature ('Tier B inflects in week 7') saves a paragraph of caption. Captions get skipped; on-chart annotations don't.

blocks.title: The translation: 28 charts becomes one BLUF chart in 5 steps

steps.label: Step 1 — Write the headline first
steps.body: Before drawing anything: write the one-sentence answer. 'Churn rose from 6.8% to 8.4% in Q3, driven by Tier B (61% of the lift).' That sentence is the chart's only job.

steps.label: Step 2 — Pick the visual gestalt that matches the sentence
steps.body: Lift over time → line chart. Comparison of two groups → side-by-side bars. Composition of a whole → stacked or treemap. Match the gestalt to the verb in the headline.

steps.label: Step 3 — Highlight only what you mean
steps.body: Reduce everything not in the headline to grey. Use one bright colour for the variable that proves the point. Five bright colours = five conclusions = no conclusion.

steps.label: Step 4 — Annotate on-chart, not in the caption
steps.body: Captions get skipped. Annotations get read. Add a short on-chart label pointing at the inflection or the gap that supports the headline.

steps.label: Step 5 — Delete the rest
steps.body: Every other chart you produced goes in the appendix. The reader who wants more will scroll. The reader who does not, you have already served.

blocks.prompt: Your headline is 'Bengaluru SaaS retention dropped 5pp in Q3, mostly in the SMB segment'. Which BLUF chart fits?

choices.label: A line chart of retention over time, with the SMB line in red and other segments in grey, and an annotation arrow pointing at the Q3 drop
choices.explain: Correct. Visual gestalt matches the headline (drop over time + segment isolation). One bright colour, one annotation, conclusion in 5 seconds.

choices.label: A heatmap of retention by city × month with all 17 cities and 12 months
choices.explain: Heatmap with 200 cells dilutes the message. The point is SMB segment, not city geography.

choices.label: A scatterplot of retention vs ARPU per account
choices.explain: Wrong axis. The headline is about time + segment, not the relationship between two metrics.

choices.label: A pie chart of segment composition
choices.explain: Pie charts are mostly bad and they cannot show change over time. Wrong tool for this headline.

hi-IN.title: Cricket commentator vs Reuters headline
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, news ka style dekh. Reuters headline: *"India GDP grows 6.4% in Q2, slowest in 8 quarters."* Sentence one mein number, direction, context. Done.

Analyst ka style: *"After careful analysis of multiple data sources spanning the period from April to June 2026, accounting for various seasonal adjustments and methodological considerations, we find that GDP growth was 6.4%."* Saaaaaaaaab kuch us se pehle, asli baat slide 7 pe.

**Reuters ka style chura. Sentence 1 mein number, direction, context. Slide 7 ki kahaani slide 1 pe le aao.**

en.title: Reuters headline vs analyst preamble
en.md: Reuters: 'India GDP grows 6.4% in Q2, slowest in eight quarters.' Number, direction, context, all in sentence one. Most analyst memos: three paragraphs of methodology, then the number on page two. Steal the Reuters opening. Move the answer to sentence one and the methodology to the appendix.

blocks.caption: Watch (~30s) · Where the eye lands on your chart — heatmap of where eyes go.

blocks.md:
BLUF gets you read. The **assumption-ledger appendix** gets you defended.

A stakeholder who acts on your number will, weeks later, be challenged on it. ('Why is your churn 8.4% when sales says 6.4%?', 'Why did you exclude trial users?', 'Why did you cohort by signup date?'). If you do not have an assumption ledger they can hand to the challenger, you become the bottleneck for every meeting where the number comes up. If you do, the ledger does the defending and you can take the day off.

The ledger goes at the *end* of the memo, never the front. Six to eight lines. Each line: the decision, the reason, the sensitivity (what would the headline number become if you reversed this decision?). The sensitivity column is the part most analysts skip and the part stakeholders care about most — because it tells them which assumptions are load-bearing and which are cosmetic.

coach.role: Tech lead at a Bengaluru SaaS, 9 years of cleaning other people's data

intro: Six common moves analysts make in their writeups. Tell me each is **good craft**, **defendable but lazy**, or **memo-killer** (the artifact will not get read or acted on).

scenarios.situation: First sentence of memo: 'Q3 churn rose from 6.8% to 8.4%; recommend pricing review by Nov 1.' Then a chart, then a ledger.
scenarios.explain: BLUF: number, direction, recommended action, all in sentence 1. Then chart proves it, ledger defends it. Standard issue.

scenarios.situation: First sentence of memo: 'In Q3 2026 we conducted a comprehensive analysis of customer attrition leveraging multiple data sources to derive insights.' Headline number is in paragraph three.
scenarios.explain: Buried lead. CFO has stopped reading by paragraph two. The analysis is fine; the artifact is dead.

scenarios.situation: Memo includes 11 charts, none highlighted.
scenarios.explain: Eleven charts of equal weight = no signal. The reader cannot tell which one matters. One BLUF chart and ten in appendix is the right mix.

scenarios.situation: Memo has a BLUF and a chart but no assumption ledger; analyst is in the meeting to defend.
scenarios.explain: Works while the analyst is in the room. The moment the memo gets forwarded, no defence travels with it. Always include the ledger.

scenarios.situation: Ledger has 6 entries, each with decision + reason, but no sensitivity column.
scenarios.explain: Halfway there. The sensitivity column ('what would change if reversed') is what stakeholders use to decide which assumptions are load-bearing. Without it, the ledger is descriptive, not defensible.

scenarios.situation: Memo opens with 'It depends — here are five scenarios with different conclusions'.
scenarios.explain: 'It depends' without a default recommendation is decision-by-handoff. State your best guess, list what would flip it, but commit to a recommendation. Otherwise the stakeholder picks one of your five at random.

blocks.title: The classic trap: ship the model, not the story
blocks.md:
The trap that gets the most analysts: building a 92%-accurate model and assuming the *number* is the deliverable. The number is the input to the deliverable. The deliverable is a story a non-analyst can act on, with a defensible record of how the number got there.

Analysts who ship the model and not the story produce work that is technically correct and operationally invisible. The model sits in a notebook nobody opens. The dashboard gets bookmarked and never returned to. The Slack message with 'analysis attached.pdf' gets a 👍 emoji and a quiet decision-by-vibes in the meeting that follows. 

The fix is unglamorous: spend the last 20% of every project on the artifact. BLUF, one chart, one ledger, one paragraph the CFO can forward. If the analysis took 4 weeks, give the writeup half a day. The 4 weeks of work landing in 90 seconds of stakeholder reading is the entire point of the job.

blocks.prompt: Order the steps of writing a memo that lands, from first to last.

items.label: Write the one-sentence headline (number, direction, action)
items.detail: Before any draft. The whole memo is built around this sentence.

items.label: Pick the BLUF chart that proves the headline
items.detail: One chart. Highlight what you mean. Annotate on-chart.

items.label: Write the supporting paragraph (3-5 sentences max)
items.detail: How the headline is supported, with the effect size and CI in plain English.

items.label: Write the recommendation (what to do, by when, with what threshold)
Edit ruthlessly: delete every sentence that does not earn its keep
items.detail: Memos shrink in revision; they do not grow.

blocks.hint: Steps 1 and 2 are inseparable; the chart and the headline are written together. Step 6 is the one most analysts skip and the one that triples readability.

blocks.instruction: You ran an analysis: SMB customers in Hyderabad use the product 18% less than 6 months ago (signed-rank test, p=0.002, 95% CI: −24% to −12%). Threshold for action was −10%. Write a 3-sentence BLUF + 1-sentence recommendation that a CFO could forward.
blocks.expected:
Headline: SMB customers in Hyderabad are using the product 18% less than 6 months ago, comfortably below our −10% action threshold.
Support: Median weekly active sessions per Hyderabad SMB account dropped from 24 to 19.6 between April and October 2026, with a 95% CI on the change of −24% to −12% (Wilcoxon signed-rank, p = 0.002).
Confidence: The CI is fully below threshold and the sample (n = 1,847 accounts with continuous activity over both periods) is large enough that this is unlikely to be measurement noise.
Recommendation: Brief the SMB success team this week to identify Hyderabad-specific churn drivers; propose a targeted intervention proposal by Nov 30, 2026.

hi-IN.title: CFO ne 'just tell me the number' bola
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, scene yeh hai. Tu ne 11-page memo bheji 'Q3 Churn Analysis'. CFO ne reply kiya: *"Just tell me the number."* 

Tu offended ho gaya — *"madam, methodology padhi nahi?"*. Madam ne padhi nahi, kyunki tu ne **artifact wrong banaya**. Madam impatient nahi hui. Madam ka time tujhe 11-page memo padhne ka nahi tha. **Tu BLUF nahi likha. Tu ne report likha.**

Reply: 3 lines. Number, recommendation, link to full memo as appendix. CFO khush, tu khush, board update Thursday ko nikla. **Length aapke insurance ke liye hai. BLUF unke information ke liye hai.**

en.title: 'Just tell me the number'
en.md: Your CFO sent back the 11-page memo with one comment: 'Just tell me the number.' She is not impatient; you produced the wrong artifact. The fix is a 3-line reply with the number, the recommendation, and a link to the long memo as appendix. Length is the analyst's insurance; BLUF is the stakeholder's information. Different products.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The 14-Page PDF Nobody Read
blocks.source: Anonymous principal data scientist at Vahan Insure, a Hyderabad-based motor-insurance startup
blocks.story:
On April 3, 2024, the data-science team at Vahan Insure delivered what they considered their magnum opus: a **14-page PDF** titled *"Q1 Claims Risk Model: Methodology, Performance, and Recommendations."* It contained 22 figures, 6 tables, 4 SHAP plots, a section on hyperparameter sensitivity, and — buried on page 11, paragraph 3 — the actual recommendation: *raise the premium for self-driven two-wheelers in three specific districts by 8 to 12 percent.*

The PDF went to the CFO, the Chief Underwriter, the COO, and the founder. The team scheduled a 60-minute readout. The founder cancelled. The COO skimmed page one, asked for 'the headline,' got pointed to page 11, and gave up at the SHAP waterfall on page 8. The Chief Underwriter, who actually had the authority to act on the recommendation, read the executive summary, found it was eight bullets long with no clear ask, and forwarded it to her team with the note *"thoughts?"*

Three weeks went by. The recommendation was never actioned. On April 24, the project was quietly killed in the next quarterly planning meeting — not because the model was wrong, but because no decision-maker could find the answer inside the artefact. The principal DS later said, in a beer-fuelled offsite confession in May: *"We spent four weeks on the model and 90 minutes on the memo. We had it backwards."*

The model was technically excellent. The communication was a 14-page coffin.
blocks.takeaway: An unread analysis is indistinguishable from an analysis that was never done. The memo is the deliverable; the model is the input.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: The CFO's Memo
blocks.setup:
It's **Week 18**. Aditi's churn investigation from Week 1 has snowballed. She's done the cohort analysis, the proper hypothesis tests, the modelling, the segmentation. She has 38 charts, 4 SQL queries that would make a senior engineer weep with joy, and a clear story.

The CFO emails at **6:14pm Thursday**: *"Board call is Tuesday at 9am. Need a memo from you on Q3 churn — what's happening, why, what we should do. Two pages max. I'll read it Monday morning."*

Aditi opens a blank Google Doc. Her cursor blinks. She has 90 hours, the work of three months, and two pages. She pings you.

coach.name: Head-of-Data Hema
coach.role: Head of Data, has watched too many brilliant analyses die in 14-page PDFs

stages.prompt: Aditi types the first heading: *"1. Methodology."* She's about to walk through her cohort approach. **Stop her.** What goes first in a board memo?

options.label: "Methodology first — they need to trust the process before they trust the number."
options.explain: This is the Vahan Insure tombstone from the field notes. Page 11 of 14. The CFO will not read past 'methodology' on a Monday morning. Methodology is an appendix, not a lede.

options.label: "BLUF — Bottom Line Up Front. The first sentence answers the CFO's question. The next sentence says what to do about it."
options.explain: **Yes.** Aditi rewrites: *"Q3 churn rose from 4.1 to 4.6 percent, driven entirely by the June referral cohort. Cohort-adjusted retention is flat. Recommendation: tighten referral-source filters; do not change retention strategy."* Two sentences. CFO knows the answer before paragraph two.

options.label: "Start with a chart that shows the trend."
options.explain: Charts are evidence, not headlines. A board reader looking at a trend chart still has to do the interpretation work. Tell them the answer; let the chart confirm it.

options.label: "Start with what changed since the last board memo on this topic."
options.explain: **Smart for a recurring memo.** Board members read in series; they want the delta from last quarter, not the full re-establishment of context. Pair this with a BLUF and you have an executive-grade opening.

stages.prompt: After the BLUF, Aditi has roughly 1.5 pages left. **What are the three sections that earn their space?**

options.label: (1) Methodology in detail, (2) all 38 charts, (3) appendix with SQL queries.
options.explain: This is exactly the 14-page PDF that didn't get read. Detail belongs in the appendix link. The memo is for decisions, not for showing your work.

options.label: (1) The evidence (one or two charts max), (2) the assumptions and what would change the conclusion, (3) the recommendation with a clear next step and owner.
options.explain: **Memo gold.** Evidence proves the BLUF. Assumptions show your honesty (and pre-empt the CFO's pushback). The recommendation makes the memo *actionable*. A board member can read this in 90 seconds and walk into Tuesday's meeting prepared.

options.label: (1) Cohort breakdown, (2) statistical significance, (3) modelling approach.
options.explain: This reads like a thesis abstract. The CFO doesn't care about your modelling approach in the body; she cares whether to act and on what. Move it to the appendix.

options.label: (1) Evidence, (2) what we'd need to be wrong, (3) recommendation, (4) what we'll know by next quarter.
options.explain: **Even better.** Adding 'what would change my mind' (assumptions/falsifiers) and 'what we'll know by next quarter' (a follow-up commitment) signals senior-analyst maturity. The board now trusts you to update them on your own claims.

stages.prompt: Aditi has the structure. She's writing the recommendation. She drafts: *"We should consider possibly tightening referral filters, subject to further analysis."* **Edit it.**

options.label: Leave it. Hedging is professional.
options.explain: Hedging like that gets read as 'the analyst doesn't know.' The CFO has read 200 of these. She wants you to take a position, with the assumptions called out. 'Subject to further analysis' is the death-rattle of any recommendation.

options.label: "Tighten referral filters to exclude the three highest-CAC partner sources by June 1. Owner: Growth team. We expect a 0.5 to 1.0 point reduction in headline churn within two cycles. If churn does not move, escalate for a deeper segmentation review."
options.explain: **A real recommendation.** Specific action, owner, deadline, expected effect, falsifier (what would prove you wrong). The board can either approve, push back on a specific element, or hand it to Growth on Tuesday afternoon. That is what a memo is for.

options.label: "Recommend further investigation into referral cohort dynamics over Q4."
options.explain: This means 'I want more time.' If you needed more time, the memo should say so explicitly with a date. Otherwise it sounds like the analysis didn't reach a conclusion — even though it did.

options.label: "Tighten referral filters by June 1. Caveat: assumes June referral cohort is the dominant driver, which holds in this analysis but should be re-verified after the August cohort lands."
options.explain: **Honest and decisive.** Takes a clear action, names the load-bearing assumption, schedules its own re-check. The CFO can sign off without doing the analyst's worrying for her.

outcomes.perfect: You took Aditi's three months of work and helped her translate it into the two pages that decide whether it ships. BLUF, evidence, assumptions, decision-grade recommendation. Tuesday's board call: the CFO opens with Aditi's recommendation verbatim. The action ships by June 1. Hema framed an internal screenshot of the memo as the team standard. Aditi's first 90 days have a closing chapter.
outcomes.good: Most of the structure is right. Drill the **recommendation specificity** — generic recommendations are how brilliant analyses become quarterly archive material. Re-read the section on owner / deadline / falsifier as the unit of an actionable ask.
outcomes.learn: Aditi sent a methodology-first memo with a buried recommendation. The CFO skimmed page one, asked for the headline, gave up, and the project quietly died in next quarter's planning. Re-read the lesson — especially the sections on **BLUF**, **assumptions over precision**, and **recommendations that ship**. The Vahan Insure 14-page PDF is not a cautionary tale. It is a forecast.

blocks.caption: Try (~60s) · Build the one-pager — drag headline, chart, recommendation into the right order.

points: Most analysis dies in the inbox because the artifact is wrong, not because the analysis is wrong; ship for 90-second reads, not for completeness.
BLUF is non-negotiable: sentence 1 is the answer, the recommendation, or both; methodology is appendix.
One chart per memo, and that chart must visually prove the headline in 5 seconds — highlight what you mean, annotate on-chart.
The assumption-ledger appendix is your defence when you are not in the room; without the sensitivity column, the ledger is descriptive, not defensible.
Spend the last 20% of every project on the artifact; the four weeks of analysis only matter if they land in the 90 seconds the stakeholder gives you.

blocks.prompt: Pick the last memo or deck you sent. Read sentence one. If a stakeholder stopped after that sentence, would they know what you found and what you recommend? If not, write the BLUF version of sentence one now.

assessment.title: Data Science and Analysis Assessment
assessment.description: Tests whether you can frame a question, clean honestly, run the right test, build the simplest model that works, and write a memo a CFO would actually read.

questions.stem: Your CMO at a Mumbai fintech says "figure out why retention dropped last quarter". What's the right first move?

choices.label: Pull the retention table and start eyeballing cohorts
choices.explanation: Tempting, and what most analysts do. You will spend 4 hours and surface 12 things that look interesting but answer no question.

choices.label: Restate the question as a testable hypothesis with a numeric definition of 'retention' and 'dropped', then ask the CMO to confirm
choices.explanation: Correct. The always-state-the-question rule. 'Retention' has at least four definitions and 'dropped' could mean 0.5 or 5 percentage points. You answer the wrong question if you skip this step.

choices.label: Build a churn model immediately
choices.explanation: Modeling before framing. You will fit a model to the wrong target and explain it confidently.

choices.label: Ask Claude to summarise the dataset
choices.explanation: Replaces your judgment with a confident-sounding paragraph. The CMO did not ask for a summary.

questions.stem: Pick the TWO things that should always go in your assumption ledger before you publish any number.

choices.label: How you defined the metric (the formula, not the name)
choices.explanation: Correct. 'Active user' means three different things to three different teams. The formula is the only honest definition.

choices.label: Which rows you dropped and why
choices.explanation: Correct. Most arguments about a number are actually arguments about which rows you excluded. Write it down before someone asks.

choices.label: How long the analysis took you
choices.explanation: Not relevant to whether the number is right. Track it for your own time-management, not in the ledger.

choices.label: The colour palette of your dashboard
choices.explanation: Cosmetic. Belongs in a style guide, not a ledger.

questions.stem: Your A/B test on a Bengaluru SaaS product shows variant B converts at 5.1% vs control at 4.8%, with n=47 per arm. What do you tell the PM?

choices.label: Variant B wins, ship it
choices.explanation: Classic n=47 trap. Confidence interval is roughly 1.6% wide on each arm. The 0.3pp gap is noise wrapped in a uniform.

choices.label: Inconclusive — sample size is too small to detect a 0.3pp effect; we need n in the low thousands per arm or we are coin-flipping
choices.explanation: Correct. Power, not p-value. With this sample size you cannot distinguish a 0.3pp effect from zero. The honest answer is 'I cannot tell yet'.

choices.label: Run the test 5 more times and pool the results
choices.explanation: Variant of p-hacking. Pooling re-tests inflates the false positive rate.

choices.label: Variant A wins because the CI overlaps
choices.explanation: Overlap means inconclusive, not 'A wins'. Defaulting to control is still a decision dressed up as analysis.

questions.stem: Your model gets 94% accuracy on the validation set after 17 rounds of hyperparameter tweaks. What is the most likely problem?

choices.label: You overfit on the validation set — every tweak peeked at val performance, so 94% is closer to training accuracy than honest test accuracy
choices.explanation: Correct. The classic trap from lesson 4. The validation set has effectively become a second training set. Hold out a clean test set and your number will drop.

choices.label: The model is genuinely good
choices.explanation: Possible but unlikely after 17 rounds of selection. Treat suspiciously good numbers like suspiciously cheap flights — there is usually a catch.

choices.label: Accuracy is the wrong metric
choices.explanation: Could be true (especially with class imbalance), but the 17-tweak red flag points at validation overfitting first.

choices.label: Sample size is too small
choices.explanation: Sample size affects variance, not the validation-overfitting bias. Different bug.

questions.stem: Pick the TWO statements that describe the BLUF (bottom-line up front) approach to a results memo.

choices.label: The first sentence states the answer, the recommendation, or the decision being asked for
choices.explanation: Correct. If the CFO reads only sentence 1, she should still be able to make the call.

choices.label: Caveats and methodology go in the appendix, not the headline
choices.explanation: Correct. Methodology earns the answer; it does not hide it. Stakeholders who want it will scroll.

choices.label: Build up suspense before revealing the conclusion
choices.explanation: That is a TED talk, not a memo. Suspense is a luxury executives do not have.

choices.label: Always include all 47 charts you produced
choices.explanation: Volume is not rigour. Pick the one chart that proves the headline.

questions.stem: A junior analyst at a Hyderabad SMB firm says "p = 0.04 so the new pricing works". Best diagnosis?

choices.label: The p-value-as-decision trap — they have not stated the effect size, the confidence interval, or whether the effect is large enough to matter for the business
choices.explanation: Correct. 'p < 0.05' is a t-shirt slogan, not a decision. A statistically significant 0.2% revenue lift is not commercially significant.

choices.label: p = 0.04 means the new pricing works
choices.explanation: This is the very trap the lesson warns about. p tells you about evidence under a null, not about business decision-making.

choices.label: p must be less than 0.01 to count
choices.explanation: Arbitrary threshold-shifting. The bug is not the threshold; the bug is using p as the only input to a multi-million-rupee decision.

choices.label: Switch to Bayesian methods
choices.explanation: Different framework, same trap if you treat the posterior probability as a single number that decides for you.

questions.stem: You inherit a 47M-row events table and your manager asks for "weekly active users". What is the right next step?

choices.label: Look at the data first — sample 1,000 rows, check timestamps, user_id nulls, duplicate events, and define 'active' before writing any aggregate query
choices.explanation: Correct. The always-look-at-it rule. Aggregates lie about clean data; rows tell the truth.

choices.label: Run a SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) GROUP BY week
choices.explanation: Skips EDA. You will count duplicate user_ids, bot traffic, and test accounts as 'active'. Your number will be 18% too high and you will not know why.

choices.label: Build a dashboard first
choices.explanation: Dashboard before discovery. The classic skip-EDA trap.

choices.label: Ask the manager which definition of 'active'
choices.explanation: Better than (b) and (c), but you still need to look at the data — the manager will not know edge cases like duplicate user_ids until you show her the rows.

questions.stem: Which TWO are reasons to start with the simplest model that works?

choices.label: It establishes a baseline that any complex model has to beat by a meaningful margin
choices.explanation: Correct. If logistic regression gets 81% and your XGBoost gets 82%, the XGBoost is not paying for itself in maintenance and explainability cost.

choices.label: Simple models are easier to explain, debug, and operate in production
choices.explanation: Correct. The model that runs at 3 AM with no Slack escalation is the model that wins.

choices.label: Complex models are illegal under GDPR
choices.explanation: Not true. GDPR cares about explainability and consent, not model class.

choices.label: Simple models are always more accurate
choices.explanation: Not true. The point is they are often accurate enough, not that they are always best.

questions.stem: Your CFO sends back your 11-page churn analysis with one comment: "Just tell me the number." Best response?

choices.label: Send a 3-line BLUF: the number, the confidence range, the recommended decision; offer the 11 pages as appendix
choices.explanation: Correct. The CFO has not become impatient; you have produced the wrong artifact. The memo always opens with the answer.

choices.label: Defend the 11 pages — every section matters
choices.explanation: Maybe to you. Not to her. Length is your insurance, not her information.

choices.label: Send the executive summary only and quietly delete the rest
choices.explanation: Throws away the methodology. When she does ask 'how did you get this?' you have nothing.

choices.label: Schedule a 30-minute meeting to walk through it
choices.explanation: Adds a calendar invite to a problem that needed a 3-line message.

questions.stem: A stakeholder asks for a chart showing "month-on-month ARPU growth". Your data only has 6 months. What do you do?

choices.label: Show 5 month-on-month deltas, label the small sample, and add a note that 6 points cannot establish a trend
choices.explanation: Correct. Honest about the limitation, useful within it. Five points is not enough for a trend; it is enough for a description.

choices.label: Fit a linear regression and project for the next 6 months
choices.explanation: 5 points and a fitted line is data-science theatre. The CI on a 5-point regression is wide enough to drive a Mahindra Thar through.

choices.label: Refuse to produce the chart
choices.explanation: Not your call alone. The right move is produce-with-caveat, not refuse.

choices.label: Make up a 12-month chart from a similar product
choices.explanation: Fabrication. Career-ender at most companies and rightly so.

questions.stem: You join a team that ships the model but never the story. What is the most likely consequence?

choices.label: Stakeholders ignore the model, override it with intuition, or stop engaging with the data team altogether
choices.explanation: Correct. A 92%-accurate model nobody trusts is an artifact, not a tool. The story is not optional packaging; it is half the deliverable.

choices.label: The model becomes more accurate over time
choices.explanation: Accuracy and adoption are independent. A model can be accurate and unused for years.

choices.label: The team gets more headcount
choices.explanation: Opposite, usually. Teams that do not communicate impact get cut first in budget season.

choices.label: Compliance auditors are satisfied
choices.explanation: Auditors specifically want the story — assumptions, limitations, decisions. Skipping the story fails audits.

questions.stem: Pick the TWO situations where you should push back on the question itself rather than answer it.

choices.label: The question is unanswerable with the data you have, and the stakeholder does not know that yet
choices.explanation: Correct. Producing a number when the data cannot support it is not service; it is malpractice with a chart.

choices.label: The question implicitly assumes a definition you know is wrong (e.g. 'active' means something different to the asker than to the system)
choices.explanation: Correct. The translation moment from lesson 1. Wrong definition, wrong answer, no matter how clean the SQL.

choices.label: The question is harder than you expected
choices.explanation: Hard is not the same as ill-formed. Hard means do the work.

choices.label: You disagree with the strategy behind the question
choices.explanation: Not your call as the analyst. Push back on the question's framing, not the company's strategy.

questions.stem: Your dashboard shows revenue is up 14% week-over-week. Before you celebrate, what is the first thing you check?

choices.label: Whether last week was a holiday, a data outage, or a definition change — the noise-vs-signal lens
choices.explanation: Correct. Big jumps are most often artifacts. Always ask 'what changed' before 'what does this mean'.

choices.label: Email the CEO immediately
choices.explanation: Premature celebration is an embarrassing way to learn that a feature flag corrupted the prior week.

choices.label: Build a forecast
choices.explanation: Forecasting on potentially corrupt data is forecasting noise.

choices.label: Add more metrics to the dashboard
choices.explanation: More metrics, same dirty source. Does not address the root question.

questions.stem: You are running a t-test comparing churn rate between two cohorts (n=2,400 each). The p-value is 0.003 and the difference is 0.4 percentage points. What do you tell the business?

choices.label: Statistically significant but commercially marginal — the 0.4pp difference is real, but probably below the threshold that would justify shipping a change
choices.explanation: Correct. With n=2,400 per arm you can detect tiny effects; that does not make them business-meaningful. State both in the same sentence.

choices.label: Significant — ship the change
choices.explanation: Confuses statistical significance with practical significance. The whole point of lesson 3.

choices.label: Not significant — kill it
choices.explanation: p = 0.003 is significant by any conventional threshold. The issue is the magnitude, not the significance.

choices.label: Run a Bayesian test instead
choices.explanation: Different framework, same answer. The honest read is 'real but small'.

questions.stem: What is the right train/val/test split discipline taught in this course?

choices.label: Hold the test set out completely until the final reported number; tune only on validation; never let test influence training decisions
choices.explanation: Correct. The test set is the audit. If you peek, you have lost the audit.

choices.label: Use the test set for hyperparameter tuning
choices.explanation: Direct violation of the lesson 4 rule. Now you have validation; you no longer have a test set.

choices.label: Skip the validation set if data is small
choices.explanation: Cross-validation exists for small data. Skipping validation entirely is overfitting on test by another name.

choices.label: Always use 80/10/10
choices.explanation: Cargo-cult ratio. Splits depend on data size, class balance, and the question. The rule is 'hold test out', not 'use this number'.

questions.stem: Pick TWO things that distinguish a memo a CFO will read in 90 seconds from one she will not.

choices.label: Headline is the answer or the recommendation, not the methodology
choices.explanation: Correct. BLUF. Methodology earns the answer; it does not lead with it.

choices.label: One chart that visibly proves the headline, not seven that decorate it
choices.explanation: Correct. The BLUF chart. One chart that pays for itself; the rest go in the appendix.

choices.label: Detailed footnotes on every regression coefficient
choices.explanation: Belong in the appendix. CFO does not need them in the headline.

choices.label: An animated GIF of the model training
choices.explanation: No CFO has ever asked for this.

questions.stem: A junior analyst writes you: "Should I just run every test and report the one with p < 0.05?" Best answer?

choices.label: No — that is p-hacking. Pre-register the hypothesis and the test before running anything; multiple-test correction if you must run several
choices.explanation: Correct. The classic trap from lesson 1. Running 20 tests at α=0.05 means roughly 1 in 20 will look significant by chance; reporting only that one is statistical fraud, even if accidental.

choices.label: Yes, if it is the only one that supports the hypothesis
choices.explanation: Definitionally p-hacking. Unethical and gets caught in code review, peer review, or the CTO Slack.

choices.label: Only if you tell the stakeholder which test you ran first
choices.explanation: Disclosure helps but does not fix it. The bug is the search-then-report pattern.

choices.label: Only if you have a Bayesian prior
choices.explanation: Frameworks do not save you from p-hacking. Pre-registration does.

questions.stem: Which is the LEAST useful response when a stakeholder asks 'is this significant?'

choices.label: "p = 0.04" with no further context
choices.explanation: Correct. The p-value-as-t-shirt-slogan trap. Tells the stakeholder nothing about effect size, confidence interval, or business meaning.

choices.label: "The 95% CI is +0.2pp to +0.9pp; the effect is real but smaller than what we agreed would justify a change"
choices.explanation: This is the recommended response: CI + business threshold.

choices.label: "What threshold of effect would change your decision?"
choices.explanation: Excellent push-back; sets the goalposts before the math.

choices.label: "We have a real but small effect (~0.5pp), and given our cost-of-shipping it is below threshold"
choices.explanation: Combines effect size, direction, and decision context.

project.title: Capstone: The Q3 Churn Memo
project.prompt:
Your CFO at a Mumbai-based fintech walks into your cubicle on Monday morning, drops a USB stick on your desk and says:

*"Spreadsheet titled 'Q3 churn — figure out why'. I have a board meeting Thursday. Tell me what's going on. One page. No PhD theatre."*

The spreadsheet is real (12,847 rows of monthly user-cohort data, three columns of definitions that don't quite agree, one column called 'flag' with 41% nulls). You have until Thursday.

Produce a one-page memo with:

1. **The hypothesis** — restate the CFO's vague ask as one testable hypothesis. Define 'churn' numerically. State what 'why' means here (which factor moved most). If the data cannot answer the question as asked, say so in the first paragraph and propose what it can answer.
2. **The evidence** — one chart and one number that prove (or fail to prove) the hypothesis. Include sample size and confidence interval. If the answer is 'we cannot tell yet', that is allowed if defended.
3. **The decision** — your recommendation in one sentence. Either ship a change, run a follow-up, or kill the question. No 'it depends' without saying what it depends on.
4. **The assumption ledger** — a 4-6 line appendix listing how you defined the metric, which rows you dropped and why, what the 41% nulls turned out to be, and the one assumption that, if wrong, would flip your recommendation.
5. **The edge** — one paragraph on what could be wrong with this analysis: a confounder you cannot rule out, a definition disagreement, a sample-size limitation, or a data-collection bug.

The memo should be the kind of thing the CFO can forward to the board with one line. Specific numbers, not vibes. No 'we observed a trend'. No 'further analysis recommended' as a placeholder for 'I did not finish'.

levels.label: Hypothesis is testable and well-defined; chosen test or comparison is appropriate; CI and effect size are reported correctly; conclusion is supported by the numbers shown
Hypothesis is reasonable; test is mostly right; one of CI / effect size / sample size is missing or off
Conclusion does not follow from the evidence, or evidence is misinterpreted (p-hacking, validation overfitting, etc.)
BLUF in the first sentence; one chart that proves the headline; assumption ledger is concrete (formulas, drop rules); memo reads in 90 seconds
Mostly BLUF but conclusion buried below paragraph 1; chart present but cluttered; ledger is partial
Wall of text; chart is decorative; no ledger; reads as analysis-by-paragraph
Names at least one specific confounder or limitation; explicitly states what would flip the recommendation; honest about the 41% nulls and the definition disagreement
Acknowledges limitations generically ('caveats apply'); does not name a specific flip condition
